314:
Diagnosis: alcohol-associated fatty liver (hepatic steatosis, or fatty change).

  • Hepatic steatosis is an early, predictable effect of alcohol consumption.
  • Lipid droplets accumulate in hepatocytes, coalesce into large droplets, distend the hepatocyte and push the nucleus aside.
  • Macroscopically the fatty liver of chronic alcohol use disorder is enlarged, soft, yellow and greasy.

Future consequences

  1. Fatty change is completely reversible if there is abstention from further intake of alcohol.
  2. With continued injury, alcohol-associated hepatitis (steatohepatitis) may develop, with ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory hyaline (skeins of keratin intermediate filaments), neutrophils and spotty necrosis or apoptosis.
  3. Fibrosis follows, starting as pericellular fibrosis with a "chicken wire" appearance. It progresses to portal and periportal fibrosis, bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis, which is often micronodular (Laennec cirrhosis, the micronodular cirrhosis of alcohol-associated liver disease).
  4. Early scarring can regress with cessation of alcohol use, but complete regression of alcohol-associated cirrhosis is rare.
  5. Only 10% to 15% of patients with alcohol use disorder develop cirrhosis.
  6. Hepatocellular carcinoma occurs mostly in chronic liver disease with cirrhosis, and alcoholic liver disease is one of the most common underlying diseases.
277: Cellular ageing is the result of a progressive decline in cellular function and viability caused by genetic abnormalities and the accumulation of cellular and molecular damage due to the effects of exposure to exogenous influences.
278:
Cellular ageing results from a combination of accumulating cellular damage (for example by free radicals), reduced capacity to divide (replicative senescence), reduced ability to repair damaged DNA, and defective protein homeostasis.

  1. Accumulation of DNA damage
    • Exogenous (physical, chemical and biologic) agents and endogenous factors such as ROS threaten the integrity of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. Most damage is repaired, but some persists and accumulates as cells age.
    • The average haematopoietic stem cell suffers 14 new mutations per year.
    • Werner syndrome (a premature ageing syndrome) is caused by a defective DNA helicase, which leads to rapid accumulation of chromosomal damage.
    • In Bloom syndrome and ataxia-telangiectasia the mutated genes encode proteins involved in repairing double-strand breaks in DNA, and patients show some manifestations of ageing at an increased rate.
  2. Replicative senescence: all normal cells have a limited capacity for replication, and after a fixed number of divisions they become arrested in a terminally nondividing state.
    • Telomere attrition: when somatic cells replicate, a small section of the telomere is not duplicated, so telomeres become progressively shorter. The chromosome ends are then seen as broken DNA, which signals cell cycle arrest.
    • Telomere length is maintained by telomerase, which is expressed in germ cells, present at low levels in stem cells and absent in most somatic tissues. In immortalised cancer cells telomerase is usually reactivated.
    • Activation of tumour suppressor genes: particularly the CDKN2A locus. Expression of its product p16 (INK4a) correlates with chronological age. By controlling G1 to S phase progression it pushes cells along the senescence pathway.
  3. Defective protein homeostasis
    • Normal folding of proteins (mediated by chaperones) and degradation of misfolded, damaged or unneeded proteins by the autophagy-lysosome and ubiquitin-proteasome systems are both impaired with ageing.
    • Mutant mice deficient in heat shock protein chaperones age rapidly, and those that overexpress such chaperones are long lived.
    • Rapamycin, which inhibits the mTOR pathway, increases the life span of middle-aged mice.
    • Misfolded proteins may accumulate and trigger apoptosis.
  4. Dysregulated nutrient sensing: caloric restriction increases life span in all eukaryotic species in which it has been tested.
    • Caloric restriction is proposed to increase longevity by reducing the signalling intensity of the insulin and IGF-1 pathways and by increasing sirtuins.
    • Sirtuins are NAD-dependent protein deacetylases. They promote the expression of genes that increase longevity: they inhibit metabolic activity, reduce apoptosis, stimulate protein folding and counteract the harmful effects of oxygen free radicals. Sirtuin-6 also promotes genomic integrity by activating DNA repair enzymes.
  5. Persistent inflammation is also among the best described mechanisms that promote cellular ageing.
384:
Acute inflammation is the likely diagnosis in both children. Pain, redness, warmth and swelling are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation. The mediators of pain are prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P, and the mediators of swelling are histamine, serotonin, C3a and C5a, and leukotrienes.

Likely diagnosis

  • 15-year-old girl, leg: acute inflammation of the leg, most probably purulent (suppurative) inflammation due to pyogenic bacteria such as staphylococci, which may form an abscess.
  • 10-year-old boy, right inguinal region, 7 days: acute inflammation of the inguinal lymph nodes (lymphadenitis), secondary to infection in the area drained. The nodes are enlarged because of hyperplasia of the lymphoid follicles and increased numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages. Red streaks on the skin represent inflamed lymphatic channels (lymphangitis).

385:
The most probable diagnosis is acute appendicitis. The diagnosis on histology requires neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria, and the blood shows neutrophilic leucocytosis.

Diagnosis

  • Acute appendicitis is most common in children and adolescents.
  • It is initiated by increased pressure in the lumen, which compromises venous outflow. Obstruction of the lumen, usually by a faecolith, is found in 50% to 80% of cases. Stasis of luminal contents allows bacteria to proliferate, which leads to ischaemia and inflammation.
  • Typically there is periumbilical pain that localises to the right lower quadrant, followed by nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever.

Expected histological findings

  • Early: congested subserosal vessels, with a modest perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate in all layers of the wall. Mucosal neutrophils and focal superficial ulceration are often present but are not specific.
  • Diagnostic: neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria.
  • More severe: a prominent neutrophilic exudate that produces a serosal fibrinopurulent reaction. Focal abscesses may form in the wall (acute suppurative appendicitis).
  • Advanced: ischaemia, haemorrhagic ulceration and gangrenous necrosis (acute gangrenous appendicitis), which may be followed by rupture and suppurative peritonitis.

Haematological findings

  • Neutrophilic leucocytosis, as in other causes of acute inflammation. The count usually rises to 15,000 or 20,000 per microlitre, with a shift to the left.
  • Raised acute-phase proteins, such as C-reactive protein, and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
386:
The most probable diagnosis is chronic osteomyelitis of the tibia, a pyogenic infection of bone in which the draining sinus and the involucrum are characteristic.

  • Pyogenic osteomyelitis is almost always caused by bacterial infection, and Staphylococcus aureus is responsible for 80% to 90% of culture-positive cases.
  • In the acute phase the bacteria induce a neutrophilic reaction, and necrosis of bone cells and marrow follows within 48 hours. The infection spreads to the periosteum, and soft tissue abscesses may form and channel to the skin as draining sinuses.
  • The dead bone is called the sequestrum.
  • The new reactive bone forms a shell of living tissue around the infected dead bone, called the involucrum. This is the sclerosis seen on the radiograph.
  • The histological findings of chronic osteomyelitis are marrow fibrosis, sequestrum and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells.
387:
The most probable diagnosis is tuberculosis. Epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells indicate granulomatous inflammation, and tuberculosis is the prototype of a granulomatous disease caused by infection.

  • Epithelioid cells are activated macrophages with pink granular cytoplasm, and Langhans giant cells are multinucleate cells formed by the fusion of activated macrophages.
  • Tuberculosis should always be excluded as the cause when granulomas are identified. In this disease the granulomas are called tubercles and have central caseous necrosis.
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by acid-fast stain for tubercle bacilli, culture and PCR.
  • Other diseases with granulomatous inflammation are leprosy, syphilis, cat-scratch disease, sarcoidosis and Crohn disease.
388:
Chronic inflammation occurs in this lesion. The complication to be feared is squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity.

Type of inflammation

  • Chronic inflammation is a prolonged host response to a persistent stimulus. It is characterised by coexisting inflammation, tissue injury and attempted repair by scarring.
  • Proliferation of fibroblasts with angiogenesis is the picture of granulation tissue, the attempted repair.
  • The persistent stimulus here is the long history of chewing betel quid.

Complication

  • Betel quid and paan contain areca nut, slaked lime and tobacco, and many of the ingredients can give rise to carcinogens.
  • Chewing betel quid is a major regional predisposing influence for squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity.
  • Persistent chronic inflammation also causes fibrosis (scarring).
389:
The most probable diagnosis is a keloid. A keloid is a raised scar that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and does not regress.

  • Excessive formation of the components of the repair process can give rise to hypertrophic scars and keloids. Excessive collagen accumulates in a raised scar.
  • Hypertrophic scars grow rapidly and contain abundant myofibroblasts, but they stay within the boundaries of the wound and tend to regress over several months.
  • Keloids grow beyond the boundaries of the original wound and do not regress. Microscopically, thick connective tissue is deposited in the dermis.
  • Keloid formation seems to be an individual predisposition.
  • Rarely, incisional scars are followed by exuberant proliferation of fibroblasts that recurs after excision. This may be a desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis), a benign neoplasm of connective tissue.
424:
Most probable diagnosis

  • Pulmonary embolism, with pulmonary haemorrhage or infarction.
  • Embolic obstruction of small end-arteriolar pulmonary branches often produces haemorrhage or infarction.
  • Fat embolism syndrome is less likely, because it typically begins 1 to 3 days after injury.

Cause of this complication

  • Deep vein thrombosis of the leg, from which fragments of thrombus detach and are carried through progressively larger veins and the right side of the heart into the pulmonary arterial vasculature. In 70% to 80% of cases, pulmonary embolism originates from leg deep vein thrombosis.
  • Bed rest and immobilisation reduce the milking action of the leg muscles, resulting in stasis.
  • Trauma, surgery and burns not only immobilise a person but are also associated with vascular insults, procoagulant release from injured tissues, increased hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors and decreased t-PA production.
471:
Probable genetic diagnosis: Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

  • The diagnostic clinical features are flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures and epicanthic folds.
  • Down syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability.
  • Approximately 95% of cases have trisomy 21, with a chromosome count of 47.

Haematological malignancy: leukaemia.

  • There is a 20-fold increased risk of precursor B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
  • There is a 500-fold increased risk of acute myeloid leukaemias.
472:
Likely diagnosis: Turner syndrome.

  • It results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome and is characterised by hypogonadism in phenotypic females.
  • Turner syndrome is the single most important cause of primary amenorrhoea, accounting for approximately one-third of the cases.
  • At puberty there is failure to develop normal secondary sex characteristics, with reduced breast development.

Karyotype

  • Approximately 57% are missing an entire X chromosome, giving the classic 45,X karyotype.
  • Approximately 14% have structural abnormalities of the X chromosome, such as 46,X,i(X)(q10), 46,X,r(X) or deletions of part of the short or long arm.
  • Approximately 29% are mosaics, such as 45,X/46,XX.
538:
Clinical diagnosis: carcinoma of the thyroid (an advanced thyroid cancer with local invasion, or a cervical lymph node metastasis from it).

  • Most thyroid neoplasms manifest as thyroid nodules, and a neck mass can be the first sign.
  • Hoarseness, dysphagia, cough or dyspnoea suggest advanced disease.
  • Anaplastic carcinoma typically presents as a rapidly enlarging bulky neck mass with compression and invasion of neighbouring structures, causing dyspnoea, dysphagia, hoarseness and cough. It is more common in older patients (mean age 65 years).
  • Medullary carcinoma may present as a mass in the neck with dysphagia or hoarseness.

Tests to evaluate the mass

  1. Fine-needle aspiration cytology, the key test to separate benign from malignant nodules, supplemented by molecular testing when the cytology is indeterminate.
  2. Ultrasonography, by which many thyroid cancers are detected.
  3. Thyroid scintigraphy. Papillary carcinomas are cold masses, and hot nodules are almost never malignant. It is generally done only when the TSH level is low.
  4. Histology of the resected tumour, which may be the only way to diagnose high-grade differentiated and poorly differentiated carcinomas, and which shows capsular and vascular invasion in follicular carcinoma.
  5. Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) if medullary carcinoma is suspected.
  6. Staging for spread to adjacent neck structures and to the lungs.
539:
Probable diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

  • Invasive squamous cell carcinomas are nodular, show variable keratin production (hyperkeratotic scale) and may ulcerate.
  • A growth fixed to the underlying structures shows invasion, the feature that most reliably marks malignancy after metastasis.
  • Risk factors include sun exposure, chronic ulcers and draining osteomyelitis, old burn scars, industrial carcinogens (tars and oils), arsenicals, ionising radiation and immunosuppression.
  • Fewer than 5% of these tumours metastasise to regional lymph nodes.

How to diagnose

  1. History and examination, including the regional lymph nodes.
  2. Biopsy with histology. Take an incisional biopsy from the edge of the lesion. The tumour shows variable differentiation, from orderly lobules with keratinisation to highly anaplastic cells with single-cell keratinisation (dyskeratosis). Poorly differentiated tumours may need immunohistochemistry for keratins to confirm the diagnosis.
  3. Staging: spread to regional nodes and distant sites.
540:
Probable diagnosis: malignant melanoma of the foot (acral lentiginous type), with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes.

  • Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer. It shows striking variation in colour (black, brown, red, dark blue, grey) and has irregular, notched borders.
  • Acral/mucosal lentiginous melanoma occurs at non–sun-exposed sites, such as the sole of the foot.
  • Locally advanced melanomas often metastasise, and the inguinal nodes drain the foot.

How to diagnose

  1. Clinical assessment by the ABCDE warning signs: Asymmetry, irregular Borders, variegated Colour, increasing Diameter, and Evolution.
  2. Complete excision biopsy of the lesion with histology. The melanoma cells have enlarged nuclei with irregular contours, peripherally clumped chromatin and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. The vertical thickness of the excised tumour predicts the risk of spread.
  3. Immunohistochemistry: melanocytic markers such as HMB-45 and SOX10.
  4. Assessment of the lymph nodes, by fine-needle aspiration of the enlarged inguinal node or sentinel node biopsy. Even small numbers of malignant cells in a draining node worsen the prognosis.
  5. Molecular testing. All metastatic cutaneous melanomas should be tested for BRAF mutations. Acral melanomas are more likely to carry KIT mutations.
3:
Hypertension is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure, defined in Robbins as a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or more or a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or more. In about 90–95% of patients the cause is unknown (essential hypertension), and in the remaining 5–10% it is secondary to renal, adrenal or other identifiable disease. Its major complications are ischaemic heart disease and heart failure, stroke, aortic dissection and renal failure.

Blood pressure is a continuously distributed variable, and the harmful effects of pressure rise progressively with no sharp threshold. Both systolic and diastolic levels carry risk. Individuals with systolic pressures below 120 mm Hg and diastolic pressures below 80 mm Hg are normotensive, and the range of 120–130 mm Hg systolic is borderline. Lower thresholds apply when other risk factors such as diabetes coexist.

Between one-third and one-half of adults in the general population are hypertensive by these criteria, and prevalence and vulnerability to complications rise with age. Because blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by peripheral vascular resistance, sustained hypertension reflects an increase in blood volume (mostly through renal sodium retention), an increase in arteriolar resistance, or both.

Causes

  • Essential (primary) hypertension (90–95%). This is a multifactorial disorder arising from the cumulative effects of many genetic polymorphisms interacting with environmental factors. Family history, twin studies and genome-wide studies (more than 500 variants) support a genetic contribution. Heavy salt intake, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity and stress are the main environmental contributors. A common final pathway is inadequate renal sodium excretion, which expands volume, raises cardiac output and causes peripheral vasoconstriction, so that pressure is "reset" at a higher level to restore sodium balance (resetting of pressure natriuresis). Vasoconstrictive stimuli and structural thickening of the arteriolar wall add to the rise in resistance.
  • Secondary hypertension (5–10%).
  • Renal: renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension, in which reduced afferent arteriolar pressure activates renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone), glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, polycystic kidney disease and other parenchymal renal disease.
  • Endocrine: primary aldosteronism (frequently an aldosterone-secreting adenoma), Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, acromegaly, thyroid disorders, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia or licorice ingestion.
  • Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta and polyarteritis nodosa.
  • Neurologic: raised intracranial pressure.
  • Pregnancy-induced: preeclampsia.
  • Drugs and hormones: oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, tyramine-containing foods with MAO inhibitors.
  • Monogenic disorders: Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutations) and defects of aldosterone metabolism (e.g., aldosterone synthase, 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase defects).

Special clinical form. In up to 5% of hypertensive patients the pressure rises rapidly (systolic above 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 120 mm Hg), producing malignant hypertension with renal failure, retinal haemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilloedema. Untreated, it is fatal within 1–2 years. It is often superimposed on pre-existing "benign" hypertension.

Complications

  1. Vascular: Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis and damages the walls of large and medium arteries. This leads to aortic dissection and to cerebrovascular haemorrhage. In small vessels it produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous pink thickening from plasma protein leakage and increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis, narrowing the lumen) and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin" laminated thickening in severe disease, with fibrinoid deposits and necrosis in malignant hypertension), as well as necrotising arteriolitis, particularly in the kidney.
  2. Heart: Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertensive heart disease), which can lead to diastolic dysfunction, left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation, demand ischaemia, congestive heart failure and sudden death. Hypertension also increases the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60%.
  3. Brain: Cerebral infarcts and intracerebral haemorrhage (stroke), and multi-infarct dementia.
  4. Kidney: Arteriolar nephrosclerosis with glomerular scarring, progressing to renal failure.
  5. Eye: Hypertensive retinopathy.

Hypertension is usually asymptomatic until late in its course. Left untreated, roughly half of patients die of ischaemic heart disease or heart failure and about one-third of stroke, and effective antihypertensive treatment dramatically lowers these outcomes.

Arteriosclerosis is the general term for hardening and thickening of arterial walls with loss of elasticity, and it includes arteriolosclerosis, Mönckeberg medial sclerosis, fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is one specific type, an intimal plaque disease of large and medium arteries made of a lipid core and fibrous cap. Its main complications are plaque rupture with thrombosis and infarction, aneurysm formation, atheroembolism, intraplaque haemorrhage and chronic ischaemia from stenosis.

Complications of atherosclerosis

  1. Stenosis with chronic ischaemia. Slow luminal narrowing (critical stenosis at about 70–75% loss of cross-sectional area in the coronaries) causes stable angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease, intermittent claudication, mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic encephalopathy. Collateral flow can compensate when stenosis develops slowly.
  2. Acute plaque change. Rupture or fissuring, erosion or ulceration, and haemorrhage into the plaque expose thrombogenic material. The resulting thrombosis, often completely occlusive, causes acute myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction or sudden cardiac death. Thin-capped, inflamed, lipid-rich "vulnerable" plaques are most prone to rupture, often when stenosis was previously only mild to moderate.
  3. Intraplaque haemorrhage, which expands the plaque and may precipitate rupture.
  4. Atheroembolism of cholesterol-rich debris, which causes microinfarcts distally (for example in the kidneys and legs).
  5. Aneurysm formation (especially abdominal aortic aneurysm) from pressure and ischaemic atrophy of the media with loss of elastic tissue, with the risk of rupture.
4:
Atherosclerosis is a chronic intimal disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which atheromatous plaques, each with a lipid core and fibrous cap, narrow the lumen and predispose to thrombosis. According to the response-to-injury hypothesis, it begins with endothelial dysfunction, followed by lipid accumulation and oxidation in the intima, monocyte recruitment and foam cell formation, platelet adhesion, smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation, and matrix synthesis, all driven by chronic inflammation.

Pathogenesis. The contemporary view holds that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury, driven by modified lipoproteins, macrophages and T lymphocytes interacting with endothelial cells and SMCs. The sequence is as follows.

  1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction. Early lesions begin at sites of morphologically intact endothelium that show increased permeability, leucocyte adhesion and altered gene expression. The three most important causes are haemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation (toxins from cigarette smoke and hypertriglyceridaemia also contribute). Plaques localise at vessel ostia, branch points and the posterior abdominal aorta because nonlaminar flow turns off atheroprotective genes such as KLF2, whereas laminar flow keeps them on.
  2. Lipoprotein accumulation and oxidation. With chronic hyperlipidaemia, LDL accumulates in the intima and is aggregated and oxidised by free radicals from inflammatory cells. Hyperlipidaemia also impairs endothelial function directly by increasing reactive oxygen species and accelerating the decay of nitric oxide.
  3. Monocyte adhesion and foam cell formation. Monocytes adhere to the activated endothelium, migrate into the intima and become macrophages. These engulf modified LDL through scavenger receptors, which cannot be downregulated, and become lipid-laden foam cells (SMCs can become foam cells by a similar route). Uptake of modified lipid releases growth factors, cytokines and chemokines that sustain a vicious cycle of monocyte recruitment. The early lesion is the fatty streak.
  4. Inflammation. Cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids in macrophages activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, producing IL-1, which activates endothelium and recruits more macrophages and T cells. Activated T cells release interferon-γ, which further activates macrophages, endothelium and SMCs.
  5. Platelet adhesion at sites of injury, with release of PDGF and other factors.
  6. Smooth muscle proliferation and matrix synthesis. SMCs migrate from the media (or arise from circulating precursors), proliferate under the influence of PDGF, FGF and TGF, and synthesise collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. This converts the fatty streak into a mature atheroma with a fibrous cap. Lipid accumulates both within cells and extracellularly, and late calcification follows.

Infection with herpesvirus, cytomegalovirus or Chlamydophila pneumoniae has been linked to atherosclerosis only circumstantially, and a causal role is not established.
5:
An atheroma has four components: cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages and T lymphocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification in late plaques. It typically has a superficial fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. The commonest sites are the lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, then the coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries and the circle of Willis.

Composition. A typical atheroma consists of:

  • A fibrous cap at the luminal surface, made of SMCs and dense collagen, whose thickness and collagen content determine stability.
  • A cellular shoulder region beneath and lateral to the cap, containing macrophages, T lymphocytes and SMCs.
  • A necrotic core deep to the cap, containing lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters, often crystalline and seen as empty clefts after processing), debris of dead cells, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and SMCs), fibrin, organised thrombus in varying degrees and plasma proteins.
  • Neovascularisation at the periphery, and calcification in advanced lesions.

Some plaques ("fibrous plaques") consist almost entirely of SMCs and fibrous tissue and may be heavily calcified.

Sites. In descending order of severity: the lower abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries, the coronary arteries, the popliteal arteries, the internal carotid arteries and the vessels of the circle of Willis. Upper limb vessels are usually spared, as are mesenteric and renal arteries except at their ostia. Plaques favour the ostia of exiting vessels and branch points, where flow is turbulent.

Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall. It may be infectious, from direct microbial invasion, or noninfectious and immune-mediated. Noninfectious forms are classified by the caliber of the vessel mainly involved: large-vessel (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis), medium-vessel (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, thromboangiitis obliterans) and small-vessel vasculitis, which is either immune complex–mediated or ANCA-associated.

Vasculitis can be systemic or confined to a single organ, and its manifestations include constitutional symptoms (fever, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise) together with organ-specific features that depend on the vessels involved. The two basic mechanisms are direct invasion of vessels by infectious agents (e.g., Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Mucor), and noninfectious immune-mediated injury through immune complex deposition, ANCA, anti-endothelial cell antibodies, anti-GBM antibodies or autoreactive T cells. Distinguishing the two is essential, since immunosuppression helps immune forms but harms infectious ones.

The major cardiac diseases are heart failure, congenital heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis, pericardial disease, and cardiac tumours. Congenital heart disease is classified functionally into left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA), right-to-left shunts (tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection) and obstructive lesions (coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, aortic stenosis or atresia).

Major cardiac diseases. Heart disease reduces to six pathophysiologic mechanisms: pump failure, obstruction to flow, regurgitant flow, shunted flow, conduction disorders and rupture of the heart or a major vessel. The clinicopathologic groups are:

  1. Heart failure, which is the common end-point of most chronic heart disease.
  2. Congenital heart disease.
  3. Ischaemic heart disease (angina, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease, sudden cardiac death).
  4. Hypertensive heart disease (systemic, and pulmonary or cor pulmonale).
  5. Valvular heart disease (rheumatic heart disease, calcific aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse, infective and noninfective endocarditis).
  6. Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive) and myocarditis.
  7. Pericardial disease.
  8. Cardiac tumours.

Classification of congenital heart disease. CHD arises from faulty embryogenesis during weeks 3 to 8 and is broadly classified by the haemodynamic consequence into shunts and obstructions. About 1% of live births have a significant cardiovascular malformation, and ventricular septal defect (42%) is the most frequent.

Tetralogy of Fallot has four components: a ventricular septal defect, obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis), an aorta that overrides the VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It is the commonest cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

The first three features arise embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, and the right ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to the pressure overload. The VSD is large, with the aortic valve overriding it, so that both ventricles empty into the aorta. The severity of the right ventricular outflow obstruction determines the clinical picture. With mild stenosis the shunt may remain left-to-right with no cyanosis ("pink tetralogy"), whereas with more severe obstruction right-sided pressures reach or exceed left-sided pressures and a right-to-left shunt produces cyanosis.

The heart is classically boot-shaped because of right ventricular hypertrophy, and a right aortic arch is present in about 25% of cases. The pulmonary stenosis protects the lungs from pressure overload, and right heart failure is rare because the right ventricle is decompressed through the VSD.

Ischaemic heart disease is myocardial ischaemia from an imbalance between myocardial blood supply and demand, caused in more than 90% of cases by obstructive atherosclerosis of the epicardial coronary arteries. It presents as angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease with heart failure, or sudden cardiac death.

IHD comprises a group of related syndromes resulting from myocardial ischaemia. In practice the four clinical presentations are:

  1. Angina pectoris (stable, Prinzmetal variant and unstable), in which ischaemia is transient and insufficient to cause necrosis.
  2. Myocardial infarction (MI), in which prolonged ischaemia causes cardiac necrosis.
  3. Chronic ischaemic heart disease, progressive heart failure from accumulated ischaemic damage.
  4. Sudden cardiac death, usually from a lethal arrhythmia.

Unstable angina, MI and sudden death due to acute plaque change with thrombosis are grouped as the acute coronary syndromes. In addition to coronary atherosclerosis (the dominant cause), ischaemia can result from coronary emboli, vasculitis, or spasm.

The history of exertional chest pain relieved by rest and sublingual nitroglycerin points to stable (typical) angina pectoris due to coronary atherosclerosis. The differentials are unstable angina, Prinzmetal angina and myocardial infarction, and noncardiac causes such as aortic dissection, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, oesophageal reflux and musculoskeletal pain. Myocardial infarction is diagnosed in the laboratory by raised cardiac troponin T or I, supported by CK-MB and the ECG.

Diagnosis. Stable angina is caused by chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis, usually with a lesion obstructing more than 70% of the lumen, so that perfusion is inadequate when demand rises with exertion, emotion or stress. The transient ischaemia (usually less than 15 minutes) does not cause necrosis. The pain is classically a crushing or squeezing substernal sensation that radiates to the left arm or jaw, and it is relieved by rest (which lowers demand) or nitrates (which dilate vessels and improve perfusion). Pain provoked in a reproducible manner and relieved in this way distinguishes it from infarction.

Differential diagnoses

  • Cardiac: unstable angina (pain at rest or crescendo and lasting longer), Prinzmetal angina (rest pain from spasm), acute MI (pain longer than 30 minutes, not relieved by rest or nitrates), acute pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, with a friction rub), aortic dissection (sudden tearing pain radiating to the back), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis.
  • Pulmonary: pulmonary embolism, pleurisy, pneumothorax, pneumonia.
  • Gastrointestinal and others: gastro-oesophageal reflux or oesophageal spasm, peptic ulcer, biliary colic, costochondritis and other musculoskeletal pain, herpes zoster, anxiety.

Laboratory diagnosis of myocardial infarction. MI is diagnosed by symptoms, the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI) and the detection of myocardial proteins in the blood. The test of choice is serum cardiac troponin T or I, which begins to rise within 2–4 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and stays elevated for 7–10 days. CK-MB, which rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal in 48–72 hours, is useful for detecting early reinfarction.

Myoglobin rises earliest but is nonspecific, and LDH (flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2) is now only of historical interest. Serial measurements are taken to document the rise and fall.

The main complications of MI are arrhythmias (the commonest, and the cause of early sudden death), contractile dysfunction with heart failure and cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation, myocardial rupture, pericarditis, mural thrombosis with embolism, ventricular aneurysm, right ventricular infarction, and progressive heart failure.

Nearly three-quarters of patients have one or more complications, and their likelihood depends on infarct size, location and the fraction of wall thickness involved.

  1. Arrhythmias occur in up to 90% of patients (ventricular premature beats, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, bradyarrhythmias and heart block), are maximal in the first hour, and account for most out-of-hospital deaths.
  2. Left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock. Pump function falls in proportion to the myocardium lost. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of transmural infarcts, usually when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
  3. Myocardial rupture (1–3%), most often 3 to 7 days after infarction when necrotic muscle is softest: free wall rupture causes haemopericardium and tamponade, septal rupture produces an acquired VSD, and papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.
  4. Papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation from ischaemia, later from fibrosis or ventricular dilation.
  5. Pericarditis, a fibrinous or fibrinohaemorrhagic reaction 2–3 days after a transmural infarct, and Dressler syndrome weeks later.
  6. Mural thrombosis with the risk of systemic embolism.
  7. Ventricular aneurysm, a late complication of a large anteroseptal infarct, with thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but no rupture.
  8. Right ventricular infarction accompanying posterior septal or inferior infarcts.
  9. Infarct expansion, ventricular remodeling and progressive heart failure (chronic ischaemic heart disease).

The important cardiac biomarkers are the cardiac-specific troponins T and I (the best markers), CK-MB, myoglobin and, historically, LDH. Acute MI is diagnosed by combining typical symptoms, ECG changes and a rise and fall of troponin above the reference limit.

The laboratory diagnosis rests on measuring proteins that leak from irreversibly injured myocytes after the sarcolemma loses integrity. Cardiac troponin T or I, regulatory proteins of calcium-mediated contraction, rise within 2–4 hours, peak at 24–48 hours and remain elevated for 7–10 days. With reperfusion they peak earlier and higher because of rapid washout. CK-MB rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to baseline by 48–72 hours, so it is useful for detecting reinfarction.

Myoglobin rises within 1–3 hours but is not cardiac-specific. LDH rises at 24–48 hours with a flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2 ratio, peaking at 3–6 days. Low-level troponin elevation ("troponin leak") also occurs in heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and sepsis, and large acute rises occur in myocarditis and myocardial trauma, so the clinical context and serial values matter. Supporting tests are the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI), echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality and coronary angiography.

Diagnosis. The pain is severe, lasts more than 30 minutes, is described as crushing and is accompanied by diaphoresis, and, unlike angina, it is unrelieved by rest or nitrates. This indicates acute MI, probably due to occlusive thrombosis over a disrupted atheromatous plaque (an acute coronary syndrome). Aortic dissection must be excluded, since it also causes severe pain.

Investigations and expected results

  • ECG: ST-segment elevation in the leads overlying the infarct (STEMI) when transmural, with later T-wave inversion and pathologic Q waves. NSTEMI shows ST depression or T-wave changes.
  • Cardiac troponin T or I: raised from 2–4 hours, peaking at 24–48 hours and remaining high for 7–10 days (serial sampling, with a rise and fall).
  • CK-MB: raised at 3–12 hours, peaking at about 24 hours and normalising in 48–72 hours. Myoglobin is raised early.
  • Blood tests: neutrophilic leucocytosis, raised ESR and CRP, possible hyperglycaemia, and a lipid profile.
  • Echocardiography: regional wall-motion abnormality and reduced ejection fraction, and evidence of complications (mitral regurgitation, VSD, effusion, thrombus).
  • Chest radiograph: pulmonary congestion if left ventricular failure. Mediastinal widening if dissection is suspected.
  • Coronary angiography: shows the occluding thrombus and underlying atherosclerotic stenosis, and allows reperfusion by angioplasty and stenting.

The goal of management is rapid reperfusion ("time is myocardium"), with antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, beta blockers and nitrates.

Rheumatic fever is an acute, immunologically mediated multisystem inflammatory disease that follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis by 2–3 weeks. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells directed against streptococcal M protein cross-react with host cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry). The diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria: evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.

Aetiopathogenesis. Rheumatic fever (RF) is a hypersensitivity (autoimmune) reaction to group A streptococcal antigens, not an infection of the heart itself. Streptococci are absent from the lesions. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with pericardial, myocardial and valvular antigens. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits Fc-receptor–bearing cells such as neutrophils and macrophages, and T-cell cytokines activate macrophages (for example within Aschoff bodies).

The 2–3 week delay (10 days to 6 weeks) reflects the time needed for the immune response. Only 0.3–3% of infected people develop RF, which points to genetic susceptibility. It mostly affects children aged 5–15 years and is favoured by overcrowding and poverty. The chronic valve deformity is the healing and scarring that follows repeated acute inflammation.

Diagnostic criteria (revised Jones criteria). Evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (a rising or raised ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or recent scarlet fever), plus:

The mitral valve is the valve most commonly affected
it is involved in virtually all cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease, alone in about two-thirds and together with the aortic valve in another 25%. An Aschoff body is the pathognomonic granulomatous lesion of rheumatic carditis, a focus of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells ("caterpillar cells").

Valve involvement. The mitral valve is virtually always involved in chronic rheumatic heart disease, in isolation in about two-thirds of cases and with the aortic valve in another 25%. The tricuspid valve is infrequently affected and the pulmonary valve rarely. Rheumatic heart disease is virtually the only cause of mitral stenosis, producing "fish-mouth" stenosis with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and thickened, fused tendinous cords.

Aschoff body. The Aschoff body is a distinctive lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, found in the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, in any of the three layers of the heart. It consists of an area of fibrinoid necrosis infiltrated by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and large macrophages with abundant cytoplasm (Anitschkow cells). In longitudinal section the central chromatin of these cells condenses into a slender wavy ribbon ("caterpillar cells"), and in cross-section appears like an "owl-eye." Some Anitschkow cells fuse to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells. Aschoff bodies are rarely seen in chronic rheumatic heart disease because of the long interval since the acute illness.

The complications of rheumatic fever are acute carditis with heart failure, arrhythmias and pericardial effusion (fatal in 1–2%), recurrent attacks, and chronic rheumatic heart disease, whose complications include mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis and right-sided failure.

Acute phase. Rheumatic carditis (pancarditis) can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure, and 1–2% of patients die of fulminant cardiac involvement. Fibrinous pericarditis with friction rub and effusion may occur. The arthritis is self-limited and leaves no deformity, and Sydenham chorea and skin lesions resolve. After the first attack, each streptococcal pharyngitis can precipitate a recurrence, and the valve damage is cumulative.

Chronic rheumatic heart disease (years to decades later). Healing by fibrosis produces leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickened, fused cords, causing mitral stenosis ("fish-mouth") and/or regurgitation and aortic valve disease. Consequent complications are left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation and mural thrombi with systemic thromboembolism (stroke), pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and failure, congestive heart failure, superimposed infective endocarditis, and valve calcification needing surgical repair or replacement.

The probable diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever. The history of a sore throat followed 3 weeks later by fever, migratory joint pain, a rash (erythema marginatum) and a subcutaneous nodule, together with a raised ESR and a raised ASO titre showing preceding streptococcal infection, fulfils the Jones criteria. In the heart there is pancarditis with Aschoff bodies, fibrinous pericarditis, myocarditis and verrucous endocarditis along the lines of closure of the mitral valve.

Diagnosis. The child has major criteria (arthritis, erythema marginatum rash and a subcutaneous nodule, with carditis to be sought) and minor criteria (fever, raised ESR), and the ASO titre of 500 IU/mL documents a preceding group A streptococcal infection. The latent period of about 3 weeks is characteristic of an immune-mediated reaction.

Cardiac changes. During acute rheumatic fever focal inflammatory lesions develop in the heart and the characteristic lesion is the Aschoff body, so that any of the three layers can be involved (pancarditis).

  • Pericarditis: fibrinous or serofibrinous pericarditis ("bread and butter" appearance), with a friction rub, which usually resolves without sequelae.
  • Myocarditis: scattered Aschoff bodies within the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, which may cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure.
  • Endocarditis (valvulitis): inflammation of the left-sided valves, especially the mitral, with fibrinoid necrosis in the cusps or tendinous cords. Small (1–2 mm), warty vegetations called verrucae form along the lines of closure. Subendocardial lesions exacerbated by regurgitant jets cause irregular thickenings in the left atrium called MacCallum plaques.

With repeated attacks, healing leads to chronic rheumatic heart disease: leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of chordae, which produce the "fish-mouth" mitral stenosis.

Infective endocarditis is a microbial infection of the heart valves or mural endocardium that produces vegetations of thrombotic debris and organisms, often with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissue. It is classified clinically into acute and subacute forms. Acute endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, and subacute endocarditis is caused by less virulent organisms, chiefly viridans streptococci, on previously damaged valves.

Infective endocarditis requires a susceptible valve and organisms in the blood. The vegetations are made of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells and colonies of organisms, and they may destroy the valve and extend into adjacent myocardium.

Types.

  • Acute IE: a virulent organism (chiefly Staphylococcus aureus) infects a previously normal valve, with rapid destruction, ring abscess and a stormy course.
  • Subacute IE: a low-virulence organism (chiefly viridans streptococci, 50–60% of native valve cases) infects a previously damaged valve (rheumatic, mitral valve prolapse, calcific stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, congenital defects), with an insidious course over weeks to months.
  • Special settings: prosthetic valve endocarditis (early: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus
    Late: streptococci), endocarditis in intravenous drug users (S. aureus, usually right-sided), and culture-negative endocarditis (about 10%).

Causative agents. S. aureus is the commonest cause overall. Viridans streptococci predominate in subacute disease. Other agents are enterococci, the HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), gram-negative bacilli and fungi (Candida, Aspergillus), the last two carrying about 50% mortality.

Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, which occurs secondary to cardiac, thoracic or systemic disorders. Important causes are infections (viruses, pyogenic bacteria, tuberculosis), myocardial infarction and Dressler syndrome, uraemia, rheumatic fever, SLE and other immunologic disorders, cardiac surgery, neoplasms and radiation.

Pericarditis is classified by the character of the exudate as serous, fibrinous or serofibrinous, purulent (suppurative), haemorrhagic, and caseous (tuberculous). The causes (Robbins Table 12.13) fall into groups:

  • Infectious: viruses (Coxsackie), pyogenic bacteria (by direct extension from empyema or pneumonia, or from blood), tuberculosis, fungi and parasites.
  • Immunologically mediated: rheumatic fever, SLE, scleroderma, postcardiotomy syndrome, post-MI (Dressler) syndrome and drug hypersensitivity.
  • Miscellaneous: acute myocardial infarction (2–3 days after infarction), uraemia, cardiac surgery, neoplasia (metastasis or direct extension, producing serous or haemorrhagic effusion), trauma and radiation.

Symptoms of fibrinous pericarditis are pleuritic, positional chest pain and fever, with a loud friction rub that is lost if a large effusion separates the layers. Healing may leave adhesions, or scarring leading to constrictive pericarditis, and rapid accumulation of even 200–300 mL of fluid can cause cardiac tamponade.

Generalised lymphadenopathy means enlargement of lymph nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions of the body. The important causes are systemic infections (viral, bacterial, protozoal), lymphoid and haematologic malignancies, autoimmune disorders, drug reactions and storage diseases.

Meaning. Lymphadenopathy is an abnormality in the size (usually more than 1 cm), number or consistency of lymph nodes. It is called generalised when nodes are enlarged in two or more noncontiguous (non-adjacent) groups, in contrast to localised lymphadenopathy, in which a single region that drains a particular area is involved. The distinction is clinically important, since localised enlargement usually reflects a regional infection or tumour drainage, whereas generalised enlargement implies a systemic process.

Mechanisms. Nodes enlarge because of (1) reactive hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and paracortical T-cell zones in response to antigenic stimulation, (2) infiltration by inflammatory cells in lymphadenitis, (3) infiltration by neoplastic lymphoid or metastatic cells, and (4) accumulation of macrophages laden with storage material. In children, systemic viral infections and bacteraemia often produce acute generalised lymphadenopathy.

Important causes

  • Infections: viral—infectious mononucleosis (EBV), cytomegalovirus, HIV (persistent generalised lymphadenopathy), rubella, measles, hepatitis B. Bacterial—tuberculosis, secondary syphilis, brucellosis, typhoid, plague. Protozoal and others—toxoplasmosis, kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), filariasis, histoplasmosis.
  • Neoplasms: non-Hodgkin lymphomas (especially follicular lymphoma and small lymphocytic lymphoma), Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Widespread metastases are an uncommon cause.

  • Drug reactions and serum sickness: phenytoin, allopurinol, carbamazepine, hydralazine, sulfonamides.
  • Others: lipid storage disorders (Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases), hyperthyroidism, Castleman disease, Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease, Rosai–Dorfman disease, amyloidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

The Reed-Sternberg cell is the neoplastic giant cell of Hodgkin lymphoma, derived from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. The classical cell is a large binucleate or multilobed cell with abundant cytoplasm and large, inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli, giving an "owl-eye" appearance.

Definition and origin. The Reed-Sternberg (R-S) cell is the neoplastic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma and is essential for its diagnosis. Single-cell molecular studies show clonal IGH gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation, establishing origin from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. Nevertheless, the R-S cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express most B-cell–specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes.

They constitute only a minority of cells (the tumour is more than 90% reactive lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and plasma cells), recruited by cytokines and chemokines secreted by the R-S cells.

Morphology of the classical (diagnostic) R-S cell. A large cell, 45 µm or more in diameter, with abundant, slightly basophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm. The nucleus is bilobed or multilobed—classically two mirror-image nuclei or lobes lying side by side—each with a thin, sharply defined nuclear membrane, vesicular, open (clear) chromatin, and a large, inclusion-like, eosinophilic or amphophilic nucleolus, about the size of a small lymphocyte (5 to 7 µm), surrounded by a clear halo, giving the "owl-eye" appearance.

Variants

  1. Mononuclear (Hodgkin) variant: a single nucleus with a large inclusion-like nucleolus.
  2. Lacunar cell: a cell with a delicate, folded or multilobated nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm that retracts during fixation, leaving the cell in an empty space (lacuna). Characteristic of nodular sclerosis.
  3. Lymphohistiocytic (L&H, "popcorn") variant: polypoid, multilobed nucleus with inconspicuous nucleoli, fine chromatin and moderately abundant cytoplasm. Characteristic of nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
  4. Mummified cell: a shrunken, pyknotic cell with condensed eosinophilic cytoplasm, the result of a peculiar form of cell death in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
  5. Pleomorphic or anaplastic variants: bizarre cells in lymphocyte-depleted (reticular) Hodgkin lymphoma.

Immunophenotype. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma the R-S cells are CD15⁺, CD30⁺ and weakly PAX5⁺, and negative for CD45 and for most B and T-cell markers
in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma the L&H cells are CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD45⁺ and negative for CD15 and CD30.

R-S–like cells may be seen in infectious mononucleosis, solid tumours and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so diagnosis depends on identifying R-S cells in the appropriate inflammatory background with a confirmatory immunophenotype.

637:
Most probable diagnosis: multiple myeloma

Confirmation

  1. Serum and urine electrophoresis for an M protein spike, characterised by immunofixation. Bence Jones protein in the urine.
  2. Bone marrow examination showing clonal plasma cells, usually more than 30% of the cellularity.
  3. CRAB criteria: hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions.
  4. Radiography showing punched-out lytic lesions.
638:
Diagnosis: chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)

  • Massive splenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis, with a white cell count above 100,000 per microlitre, in an adult.
  • Blood: neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Blasts usually less than 10%
    Platelets often increased.
  • Confirmed by detection of the BCR::ABL fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)) by chromosomal analysis or PCR-based tests. This separates CML from other myeloproliferative neoplasms.
639:
Clinical diagnosis: acute leukaemia, most probably acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), the most common cancer of children.

  • Weakness from anaemia
    Fever from infections secondary to neutropenia
    Gum bleeding from thrombocytopenia
    Joint and bone pain from marrow expansion and infiltration of the subperiosteum.

Expected peripheral blood film findings

  • Anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
  • Blast count highly variable
    Blasts may be absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia).
  • Lymphoblasts have condensed chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm.

Bone marrow examination is essential to confirm the diagnosis.
755:

Probable diagnosis: β-thalassaemia major.

Basis

  • Anaemia manifests 6 to 9 months after birth as haemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA. Untransfused haemoglobin is 3 to 6 g/dL.
  • Marrow expansion in facial bones and skull gives the facial change.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly from phagocyte hyperplasia and extramedullary haematopoiesis. The spleen may weigh up to 1500 g.
  • Growth retardation in untreated children.

Confirmation

  1. Blood smear: anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, microcytosis and hypochromia. Target cells, basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells. Nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts).
  2. Reticulocyte count: raised, but lower than expected for the severity of the anaemia, because of ineffective erythropoiesis.
  3. Haemoglobin analysis: HbA absent (β0/β0) or present in small amounts (β+/β+ or β0/β+). HbF is the major haemoglobin and is markedly elevated.
  4. Marrow: striking expansion of haematopoietically active marrow. "crewcut" appearance of the skull on X-ray.
  5. Iron studies: to separate from iron deficiency
    Iron overload (haemosiderosis) occurs in transfused patients.
757:
Likely diagnosis: acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

Basis

  • Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood.
  • Symptoms appear abruptly, often 1 to 2 weeks after a self-limited viral illness.
  • It is caused by autoantibodies to platelets.
  • It is self-limited, usually resolving within 6 months.

Further investigations

  1. Platelet count: low, with large platelets (megathrombocytes) in the peripheral blood.
  2. Coagulation tests: PT and PTT normal.
  3. Bone marrow: normal or increased megakaryocytes, some immature. Its importance is to rule out marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders.
  4. Exclusion of secondary causes: systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection and B-cell neoplasms.
  5. Tests for platelet autoantibodies have low sensitivity and specificity and are not clinically useful.
758:
Excessive bleeding can result from increased fragility of vessels, platelet deficiency or dysfunction, or derangement of coagulation.

  1. Vessel wall abnormalities: small haemorrhages, particularly of the gingivae
    Platelet count, PT and PTT normal. Examples are scurvy and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (collagen defects).
  2. Thrombocytopenia: immune thrombocytopenic purpura (gingival bleeding and easy bruising). Aplastic anaemia
    Marrow replacement by leukaemia.
  3. Defective platelet function: von Willebrand disease
    Inherited disorders of platelet function.
  4. Clotting factor deficiency: haemophilia A and B.
  5. Acute leukaemia: mucosal haemorrhages into the gingivae
    Monocytic leukaemias infiltrate the gingiva.
  6. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.
759:
Provisional diagnosis: haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency).

Basis

  • X-linked recessive trait, affecting mainly males
    Transmitted through carrier females, hence the affected maternal uncle.
  • Easy bruising and massive haemorrhage after trauma or surgery.
  • "Spontaneous" haemorrhages in regions susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints (haemarthroses). Recurrent bleeding leads to progressive disabling deformities.
  • Petechiae are characteristically absent.

Confirmation

  1. PTT: prolonged.
  2. PT: normal, pointing to an abnormality of the intrinsic pathway.
  3. Factor VIII assay: required for diagnosis. Severity: less than 1% of normal is severe, 2% to 5% moderately severe, 6% to 50% mild.
  4. Factor IX assay, to exclude haemophilia B (Christmas disease), which is clinically indistinguishable and also shows prolonged PTT and normal PT.
760:
Probable causes

  1. Iron deficiency anaemia: increased requirement in pregnancy
    The commonest cause.
  2. Folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia): increased requirement in pregnancy from increased DNA synthesis.
  3. Vitamin B12 deficiency: relative deficiency from increased demand in pregnancy.

Confirmation of iron deficiency

  1. Haemoglobin and haematocrit depressed, with hypochromia, microcytosis and modest poikilocytosis. Pencil cells.
  2. Serum iron and ferritin low.
  3. Total iron-binding capacity high.
  4. Transferrin saturation below 15%.
  5. Absent stainable iron in marrow macrophages, on Prussian blue stain of marrow aspirate.
  6. Reticulocyte rise in 5 to 7 days after oral iron.

Confirmation of folate deficiency

  1. Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils and low reticulocyte count on the blood film.
  2. Decreased serum or red cell folate.
  3. Raised serum homocysteine
    Methylmalonate normal.
  4. Vitamin B12 deficiency must be excluded before folate is given.

Basis

  • Ataxic gait: demyelination of the dorsal and lateral spinal tracts, giving sensory ataxia and paraesthesiae.
  • Weakness and palpitation: symptoms of anaemia.

Obstructive lung diseases are disorders characterised by an increase in resistance to airflow due to diffuse airway disease at any level of the respiratory tract. Pulmonary function tests show reduced maximal expiratory flow, with an FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.7. The obstructive diseases are chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, bronchiectasis and small airways disease (bronchiolitis), with chronic bronchitis and emphysema together forming COPD.

Obstructive disease contrasts with restrictive disease, in which expansion of the lung parenchyma is reduced and total lung capacity is decreased, with a proportionate fall in both FEV₁ and FVC so that the ratio remains normal.

29:
COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is, in the WHO definition, a common, preventable and treatable disease characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by exposure to noxious particles or gases. Its two major clinicopathologic types are emphysema and chronic bronchitis, which usually coexist, and the principal risk factor is cigarette smoking.

Types. COPD has two major clinicopathologic manifestations, emphysema (airspace enlargement with alveolar wall destruction, typically centriacinar) and chronic bronchitis (persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years), with small airway inflammation and fibrosis contributing to airflow obstruction. Because they share smoking as the main aetiologic factor, they commonly coexist in the same patient, and the clinical picture ranges from "pink puffers" (emphysema dominant) to "blue bloaters" (chronic bronchitis dominant). Asthma is distinguished by reversible bronchospasm, but some patients have overlap (COPD/asthma).

Risk factors

  • Cigarette smoking is dominant: about 80% of COPD is attributable to it, and 35–50% of heavy smokers develop COPD.
  • Exposure to environmental and occupational pollutants (dusts, gases, fumes, and also household biomass smoke).
  • Poor lung development early in life.
  • Airway hyperresponsiveness.
  • Genetic factors: α₁-antitrypsin deficiency (panacinar emphysema) and other polymorphisms (for example NRF2 pathway and nicotinic receptor variants).
  • Recurrent respiratory infections, which exacerbate but do not initiate disease.
30:
Emphysema is defined by irreversible enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of the alveolar walls. Its four types are centriacinar (the commonest and the one linked to smoking), panacinar (α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), distal acinar or paraseptal, and irregular. Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as persistent cough with sputum production for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years in the absence of any other identifiable cause.

Chronic bronchitis is characterised by hypersecretion of mucus, enlargement of the submucosal glands (increased Reid index) and goblet cell hyperplasia, with chronic airway inflammation, mainly caused by smoking (90% of cases).
31:
Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous disease characterised by chronic airway inflammation and variable, reversible expiratory airflow obstruction, producing episodic wheezing, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough. Lung diseases caused by air pollutants include chronic bronchitis, emphysema, the pneumoconioses (coal workers' pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis, berylliosis), occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and lung cancer.

Asthma. In its commonest (atopic) form, asthma is a type I hypersensitivity reaction in which a Th2 response with IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 drives IgE production, eosinophilic inflammation, bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion and, with time, airway remodeling. Episodes are triggered by allergens, viral infection, irritants, cold air, exercise and stress. Symptoms tend to be worse at night or early in the morning, and between attacks the patient may be asymptomatic. Nonatopic, drug-induced (aspirin) and occupational forms also occur.

Lung diseases caused by air pollutants

  • Obstructive diseases: chronic bronchitis and emphysema (tobacco smoke, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, dust), and occupational asthma (fumes, plastics, chemical dusts, formaldehyde).
  • Pneumoconioses: coal workers' pneumoconiosis (coal dust), silicosis (silica), asbestosis and asbestos-related pleural disease and mesothelioma (asbestos), berylliosis (beryllium).
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic dusts (e.g., farmer's lung).
  • Lung cancer from asbestos, radon, arsenic, chromium, nickel, uranium and tobacco smoke.
  • Air pollution contributes to lung irritation and inflammation, and exacerbates asthma.
32:
Interstitial lung diseases are a heterogeneous group of chronic disorders characterised predominantly by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, producing a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests with reduced lung volume, compliance and diffusing capacity. Examples include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, pneumoconioses, sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Affected patients have dyspnoea, tachypnoea, end-inspiratory crackles and eventual cyanosis, without wheezing. Chest radiographs show bilateral small nodules, irregular lines or ground-glass shadows corresponding to interstitial fibrosis. Advanced disease of any type leads to diffuse scarring ("end-stage" or "honeycomb" lung), with secondary pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

Major categories (Robbins Table 15.5):

  • Fibrosing: usual interstitial pneumonia (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organising pneumonia, connective tissue disease–associated ILD, pneumoconioses, and drug reactions or radiation pneumonitis.
  • Granulomatous: sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
  • Eosinophilic: pulmonary eosinophilia.
  • Smoking-related: desquamative interstitial pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis–associated ILD, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
  • Other: pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia.
33:
The common pulmonary infections are acute bacterial pneumonia (most often pneumococcal, with Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella and Staphylococcus aureus), tuberculosis, viral pneumonias (influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2), lung abscess and fungal infections. "Atypical" pneumonia is caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila species, Coxiella burnetii, Legionella and respiratory viruses.

The chapter does not give country-specific data, but the common infections in Bangladesh, a resource-limited setting with a heavy burden of respiratory disease, are the following.

  • Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (leading cause of childhood mortality and common in adults): Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest, followed by Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae (especially in debilitated and diabetic patients and alcoholics), Staphylococcus aureus (after influenza or measles) and Moraxella catarrhalis.
  • Tuberculosis: Bangladesh is among the high-burden countries.
  • Viral pneumonias: influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, metapneumovirus, adenovirus, and COVID-19.
  • Hospital-acquired pneumonia by gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas and MRSA.
  • Lung abscess, bronchiectasis, and fungal infections (e.g., aspergillosis) in compromised lungs.

Atypical pneumonia is a descriptive term for pneumonia with patchy interstitial inflammation, moderate symptoms and few physical signs relative to the clinical illness, in which the bacterial culture is negative. Causative organisms are Mycoplasma pneumoniae (the commonest, in children and young adults), Chlamydophila pneumoniae and C. psittaci, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Legionella pneumophila, and viruses (influenza A and B, RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, coronaviruses).
34:
Viruses that cause pneumonia include influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, rhinovirus, coronaviruses (including SARS-CoV-2), measles and varicella. The four morphological stages of lobar bacterial pneumonia are congestion, red hepatisation, grey hepatisation and resolution.

Viruses. Respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus and human metapneumovirus are important in children, influenza A and B in adults, and adenovirus in military recruits. Others are cytomegalovirus and herpesviruses (in the immunocompromised), measles (rubeola), varicella and SARS-CoV-2. Viral pneumonia is characterised by interstitial lymphocytic inflammation rather than the intraalveolar neutrophilic exudate of bacterial pneumonia, and it predisposes to bacterial superinfection ("flu condemns, and additional infection executes").

Stages of lobar pneumonia.

  1. Congestion: the lung is heavy, boggy and red, with vascular engorgement, intraalveolar oedema fluid, a few neutrophils and numerous bacteria.
  2. Red hepatisation: massive confluent exudation of neutrophils, red cells and fibrin fills the alveoli, and the lobe is red, firm and airless like liver.
  3. Grey hepatisation: red cells disintegrate while the fibrinosuppurative exudate persists, and the lobe becomes greyish-brown.
  4. Resolution: the exudate is enzymatically digested into granular semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages or expectorated, or organised by fibroblasts.
35:
Pneumonia is caused by bacteria (most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses, mycoplasma and other atypical organisms, fungi and, less commonly, parasites. Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) pneumonia is pneumonia acquired in the course of a hospital stay, most commonly caused by gram-negative rods and Staphylococcus aureus.

Aetiologic agents (these depend on the clinical setting, and no organism is identified in about 50% of cases):

  • Community-acquired: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the commonest cause), Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila species, Coxiella burnetii, and viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, influenza A and B, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2).
  • Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated: gram-negative rods (Klebsiella, Serratia, E. coli, Pseudomonas) and S. aureus (often MRSA).
  • Aspiration pneumonia: anaerobic oral flora (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) mixed with aerobes.
  • Chronic pneumonia: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and atypical mycobacteria, Histoplasma, Coccidioides and Blastomyces.
  • Immunocompromised host: Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus, Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, Pseudomonas and Legionella.

Nosocomial pneumonia is a pulmonary infection acquired during a hospital stay (generally developing 48 hours or more after admission). It is common in patients with severe underlying disease, immunosuppression, prolonged antibiotic therapy and invasive devices such as intubation, intravascular catheters and respirators (ventilator-associated pneumonia). Hospital bacteria are often antibiotic-resistant, there are more opportunities for spread, and equipment may be contaminated.

The commonest isolates are S. aureus and gram-negative rods (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas). It is serious and often life-threatening and requires broad-spectrum empirical therapy. Healthcare-associated pneumonia (from nursing homes, dialysis clinics and recent hospitalisation) is a related category, caused particularly by MRSA and P. aeruginosa.
36:
The leading differential diagnoses are acute bacterial (lobar) pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis and bronchogenic carcinoma, particularly if the consolidation does not resolve. Other possibilities are lung abscess, pulmonary infarction and (less commonly) fungal infection. I would investigate with sputum Gram stain and culture, sputum for AFB and Xpert MTB/RIF, blood cultures, a complete blood count and inflammatory markers, CT chest, and bronchoscopy with biopsy or CT-guided FNAC if a mass is suspected.

Differential diagnosis

  1. Lobar or bronchopneumonia: most commonly S. pneumoniae with abrupt fever, rigors, pleuritic chest pain and rusty sputum or haemoptysis, and with lobar consolidation (a radiopaque lobe). Klebsiella pneumonia (in alcoholics and diabetics) gives thick blood-tinged sputum and necrosis.
  2. Pulmonary tuberculosis: subacute or chronic cough, fever, weight loss, haemoptysis, with upper-lobe consolidation or cavitation in secondary TB.
  3. Bronchogenic carcinoma: in a 50-year-old smoker, with obstructive (postobstructive) pneumonia or lobar collapse and haemoptysis. Adenocarcinoma can mimic lobar pneumonia.
  4. Lung abscess (aspiration or necrotising pneumonia, often with foul sputum).
  5. Pulmonary infarction from embolism, with pleuritic pain and haemoptysis.
  6. Others: granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infection, Goodpasture syndrome and bronchiectasis.

Investigations

  • Blood: complete blood count (neutrophilic leucocytosis), ESR, CRP, blood cultures (positive in only 20–30% of pneumococcal cases early), blood glucose.
  • Sputum: Gram stain (neutrophils with lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci in pneumococcal pneumonia) and culture with sensitivity, Ziehl-Neelsen stain and Xpert MTB/RIF or culture, and cytology for malignant cells.
  • Imaging: chest radiograph (lobar versus patchy opacity, cavity, effusion) and CT chest.
  • Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings, brushings and biopsy, or CT-guided FNAC/biopsy for a mass.
  • Others: pleural fluid analysis if there is effusion, urinary Legionella antigen or PCR when indicated, arterial blood gases, and Mantoux or IGRA if tuberculosis is suspected.
  • Failure of the consolidation to resolve after adequate treatment should prompt exclusion of an underlying carcinoma.
37:
Primary tuberculosis most commonly involves the lung, where the Ghon focus is a subpleural parenchymal lesion in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, close to the pleura. Less commonly it affects the tonsils and oropharynx or the ileocaecal region of the gut (after ingestion of M. bovis in unpasteurised milk). Ghon's complex consists of the Ghon focus together with the caseating tuberculous lymphangitis and the enlarged, caseous regional (hilar) lymph nodes.

Primary sites. In primary tuberculosis, after inhalation of droplet nuclei the bacilli lodge in the alveoli of the middle zones of the lung, in the subpleural part of the lower lobe or the lower part of the upper lobe. Other sites of primary infection are the tonsil and pharynx (cervical lymph nodes) and the terminal ileum and caecum (mesenteric nodes), the latter from bovine bacilli.

Ghon's complex. The Ghon focus is a 1–1.5 cm grey-white area of inflammation with a central caseous necrosis. Bacilli drain through lymphatics to the hilar lymph nodes, which become enlarged and caseous. The combination of the parenchymal Ghon focus, lymphangitis and caseous hilar lymph node lesion is the Ghon complex. With development of cell-mediated immunity after about 3 weeks the lesion usually heals by fibrosis and calcification (Ranke complex when calcified), though viable organisms may persist and cause reactivation later.
38:
Primary tuberculosis is the infection of a previously unexposed, unsensitised person, which forms the Ghon complex, and it is often asymptomatic. Secondary (postprimary or reactivation) tuberculosis arises in a previously sensitised host, from reactivation of dormant bacilli or exogenous reinfection. The predominant site of primary TB in the lung is the subpleural zone of the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, and that of secondary TB is the apex of the upper lobes.

In primary tuberculosis there is a Ghon focus of 1–1.5 cm in the subpleural lung with central caseation, and enlarged caseous hilar lymph nodes (Ghon complex), with the characteristic tuberculous granulomas. Miliary tuberculosis is widespread haematogenous dissemination of the organisms, producing numerous tiny (millet-seed size, 2 mm) yellow-white foci in the lungs and many other organs.

Morphology of primary TB.

  • Ghon focus: a grey-white, firm area, 1–1.5 cm, in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe beneath the pleura, with central caseous necrosis. The pleural surface may have a fibrinous reaction.
  • Lymphatic spread to the hilar and peribronchial lymph nodes, which become enlarged with caseation (Ghon complex). In the gut, the corresponding lesion affects Peyer patches and mesenteric nodes.
  • Microscopy: caseating granulomas composed of a central zone of caseous necrosis (amorphous, granular, eosinophilic) surrounded by epithelioid macrophages, Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells, and a rim of lymphocytes and fibroblasts. Acid-fast bacilli can be shown by Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
  • Fate: in most patients cell-mediated immunity develops at about 3 weeks, and the lesions heal by fibrous scarring and calcification (Ranke complex). Rarely, progressive primary TB occurs, with spread to the pleura, bronchi (tuberculous bronchopneumonia), or by haematogenous route.

Miliary tuberculosis results from erosion of a focus of caseous disease into a blood vessel (or lymphatic channel draining into the venous system), which disseminates the organisms through the blood. It produces innumerable small, yellow-white foci about 2 mm in diameter (like millet seeds) in the lungs (pulmonary vein spread), or in the spleen, liver, kidneys, bone marrow, meninges, adrenals and other organs (systemic arterial spread). It may complicate primary or secondary TB, especially in infants, the elderly and the immunocompromised.
