Tuberculosis can involve virtually any organ, but it is rare in tissues such as skeletal muscle, the myocardium, the thyroid and the pancreas, which appear resistant. A granuloma is a focal collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells and a surrounding rim of lymphocytes, formed in chronic inflammation as a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to a persistent antigen.

Sites of rare involvement. Tuberculosis characteristically spares skeletal muscle and the heart (myocardium), and the thyroid and pancreas are also rarely involved, probably because of local tissue factors such as the high oxygen environment, motion and lytic enzymes, and the antibacterial milieu. Involvement of these sites is exceptional, even in miliary disease.

Granuloma. A granuloma is a distinctive pattern of chronic inflammation in which activated macrophages accumulate to form epithelioid cells ("epithelial-like" macrophages with pale pink granular cytoplasm and indistinct borders), which may fuse to form giant cells (Langhans type with nuclei in a horseshoe arrangement at the periphery, or foreign body type with nuclei scattered).

Lymphocytes (mainly CD4⁺ T cells), and sometimes fibroblasts, surround the aggregate. It is produced by a T-cell–mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity response, when IFN-γ released by Th1 cells activates macrophages, as in tuberculosis. Granulomas may be caseating, with central necrosis (tuberculosis, fungi), or noncaseating (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, berylliosis), and may also be caused by foreign bodies.

Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophageal body loses peristalsis because the inhibitory, nitric oxide–producing neurons of the myenteric plexus degenerate. it presents with dysphagia and a dilated oesophagus. Reflux oesophagitis is inflammation of the distal oesophageal squamous mucosa caused by repeated reflux of gastric contents through an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter, and it is the clinical basis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Achalasia. Achalasia is defined by a triad: incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) on swallowing, increased resting LES tone, and aperistalsis of the oesophageal body. The sphincter therefore behaves as a functional obstruction, food is retained, and the oesophagus above it dilates progressively.

Aetiology and pathogenesis. Primary achalasia is rare and idiopathic. It results from degeneration of the nitric oxide–producing inhibitory neurons that normally relax the LES. The extra-oesophageal vagus nerve and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may also show degenerative change. Rare familial cases are described, and an immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory neurons is suspected because some cases follow herpes simplex virus 1 infection, show linkage to immunoregulatory gene polymorphisms, or coexist with Sjögren syndrome or autoimmune thyroid disease.

Secondary achalasia arises when the myenteric plexus is destroyed by another process. The classic example is Chagas disease, in which Trypanosoma cruzi infection destroys the myenteric plexus (and may involve the duodenal, colonic, and ureteric plexuses as well). Other causes include diabetic autonomic neuropathy, infiltrative disorders such as malignancy, amyloidosis, and sarcoidosis, systemic sclerosis, lesions of the dorsal motor nucleus (for example after poliomyelitis), and Down syndrome.

Morphology and clinical features. The oesophagus above the sphincter is dilated, with hypertrophy of the muscularis in the early stage and thinning later. Histology shows a reduced number or absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus with a variable chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Patients have dysphagia for both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, difficulty in belching, and chest pain, and aspiration pneumonia may follow nocturnal regurgitation.

A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering to a "bird-beak" narrowing, and manometry confirms the diagnosis. Stasis oesophagitis and candidiasis may occur. There is a modestly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma, but not enough to justify surveillance endoscopy. Treatment is directed at overcoming the obstruction: pneumatic balloon dilation, botulinum toxin injection to inhibit contraction-promoting cholinergic neurons, or surgical myotomy.

Reflux oesophagitis. Reflux of gastric contents into the lower oesophagus is the commonest cause of oesophagitis and the most frequent outpatient gastrointestinal diagnosis in high-income countries. The stratified squamous epithelium is highly abrasion resistant but is sensitive to gastric acid and pepsin, and bile may add to the injury.

Pathogenesis. The major mechanism is transient relaxation of the LES, mediated through vagal pathways and triggered by gastric distention. Reflux also follows abrupt rises in intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining, bending). Predisposing conditions include alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, central nervous system depressants, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, increased gastric volume, and drugs or foods that lower LES pressure.

Morphology. Mild disease may show only hyperaemia, with unremarkable histology. More severe reflux produces erosions, basal zone hyperplasia, elongation of the lamina propria papillae, and infiltration of the squamous mucosa by eosinophils. Neutrophils appear later or when infection or chemical injury is superimposed. Chronic injury leads to ulceration, fibrosis, and stricture.

Clinical features and complications. Symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation of sour-tasting fluid, and dysphagia, most often after meals, and they may be mistaken for ischaemic heart disease. Symptom severity correlates poorly with the histologic damage. Diagnosis is usually clinical
Endoscopy is reserved for patients who fail proton pump inhibitor therapy or in whom complications are suspected.

Proton pump inhibitors relieve symptoms in up to 90% of patients. The complications are erosive oesophagitis with bleeding, ulceration, peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus, and, through Barrett oesophagus, oesophageal adenocarcinoma. A sliding hiatal hernia, in which the gastro-oesophageal junction herniates through the diaphragmatic hiatus, may impair LES competence and produce a similar syndrome.

Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus (and proximal stomach) that develop as portosystemic collaterals when portal venous pressure is raised, most commonly because of cirrhosis. They matter because large varices can rupture and cause massive, life-threatening haematemesis.

Mechanism. Portal hypertension, defined as increased resistance to portal blood flow, may be prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis or narrowing, splenic vein flow increase), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, which accounts for most cases; schistosomiasis, massive fatty change, sarcoidosis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia), or posthepatic (severe right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, hepatic vein outflow obstruction).

In cirrhosis, resistance is raised at the level of the sinusoids by scarring and nodule formation, by contraction of sinusoidal smooth muscle cells and myofibroblasts, and by endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide and increased endothelin-1. At the same time, splanchnic arteriolar vasodilation, driven chiefly by nitric oxide, produces a hyperdynamic circulation that increases portal inflow.

Because the portal system has no valves, blood seeks alternative pathways to the systemic venous circulation wherever the portal and caval systems communicate. At the gastro-oesophageal junction, blood from the left gastric (coronary) vein is diverted through the subepithelial and submucosal venous plexuses of the distal oesophagus into the azygos system. These thin-walled veins become congested and dilated, forming varices.

Varices are most common in alcohol-associated cirrhosis but complicate cirrhosis of any cause. non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (presinusoidal as in schistosomiasis, sinusoidal as in amyloidosis, postsinusoidal as in Budd–Chiari syndrome) can also produce them. They are present in about 30% of patients with compensated cirrhosis and about 60% of those with decompensated cirrhosis.

Morphology. Varices are dilated, tortuous veins within the mucosa and submucosa of the distal oesophagus and proximal stomach that bulge into the lumen under an intact, thinned mucosa. After rupture there may be mucosal ulceration, thrombosis, inflammation, and evidence of prior sclerotherapy or band ligation.

Oesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins of the distal oesophagus that form as collateral channels when raised portal pressure, usually from cirrhosis, diverts blood through the left gastric–azygos connections. Their principal complication is variceal rupture with torrential haematemesis, which is a medical emergency with a high mortality.

Definition and mechanism. Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated veins in the lower oesophageal submucosa and mucosa. They are caused by portal hypertension, which most often results from cirrhosis. Increased portal venous pressure opens collateral channels at sites where the portal and systemic venous beds communicate: the oesophagogastric junction, the anorectal junction (haemorrhoids), the falciform ligament (periumbilical veins, giving caput medusae), and the retroperitoneum.

In the oesophagus the collateral flow passes from the left gastric vein through the oesophageal submucosal plexus to the azygos vein. The plexus has little connective tissue support and dilates under the high pressure. Two factors sustain portal hypertension: increased intrahepatic (sinusoidal) resistance from fibrosis, nodule formation, and vasoconstrictor mediators, and increased portal inflow from splanchnic vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide.

Complications

  • Variceal haemorrhage is the major complication. Large or tortuous varices, high hepatic venous pressure gradient, red colour signs, previous bleeding, and advanced liver disease increase the risk of rupture. Each episode carries a mortality of roughly 15% to 20%, and more than half of survivors rebleed within one year.
  • Hypovolemic shock and death, directly from exsanguination or from precipitation of hepatic failure, since blood in the gut gives a large nitrogen load that provokes hepatic encephalopathy.
  • Infection (aspiration pneumonia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) after a bleed.
  • Renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome) after haemorrhage.
  • Ulceration, thrombosis, and stricture of the oesophageal wall after rupture, banding, or sclerotherapy.

Management comprises resuscitation, splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic variceal ligation or sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade, and, for prevention, non-selective beta-blockers and repeated ligation. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting is used for refractory bleeding.

Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux in which the normal squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus is replaced by metaplastic intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Its importance is that it is the precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and it is diagnosed by endoscopy with biopsy showing columnar mucosa with goblet cells above the gastro-oesophageal junction.

Definition and pathogenesis. Barrett oesophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the oesophageal squamous mucosa arising in the setting of long-standing GERD. Chronic exposure of the squamous epithelium to acid and bile reflux leads to replacement by a more acid-resistant columnar epithelium. It is estimated to occur in up to 10% of persons with symptomatic GERD and in about 2% of the general population
it is most common in white men between 40 and 60 years of age, and obesity (central) is a recognised risk factor.

Morphology. Endoscopically, tongues or circumferential bands of red, velvety mucosa extend upward from the gastro-oesophageal junction, alternating with residual pale, smooth squamous mucosa. The segment is classified as long (3 cm or more) or short (less than 3 cm). Histologically, the squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium of intestinal type, with goblet cells (the diagnostic feature) whose distended mucin vacuoles stain pale blue and give the cytoplasm the shape of a wine goblet, along with non-goblet columnar cells.

Dysplasia, graded as low or high, is characterised by nuclear hyperchromasia, stratification, loss of polarity, irregular budding glands, and gland-within-gland architecture. Invasion into the lamina propria defines intramucosal carcinoma.

Clinical importance

  1. It is the only recognised precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Most adenocarcinomas arise in Barrett oesophagus, although most patients with Barrett oesophagus never develop cancer.
  2. The cancer risk is greatest with goblet-cell metaplasia, long-segment disease, increasing age, male sex, and especially the presence and grade of dysplasia.
  3. Because dysplasia is a treatable preinvasive stage, Barrett oesophagus justifies surveillance endoscopy and biopsy, and dysplasia may be treated by radiofrequency ablation or endoscopic mucosal resection.
  4. It also signifies long-standing reflux disease and may be complicated by ulcer and stricture.

Diagnosis. The diagnosis is made by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which demonstrates columnar-lined mucosa extending above the gastro-oesophageal junction, followed by systematic biopsy (four-quadrant biopsies at regular intervals along the segment plus targeted biopsies of any visible lesion). Histology confirms intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (highlighted by Alcian blue at pH 2.5), and the biopsy must be assessed for dysplasia. a diagnosis of high-grade dysplasia is usually confirmed by a second pathologist. Chromoendoscopy or narrow-band imaging increases the yield of surveillance biopsies.

Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, recognised histologically by the presence of neutrophils or chronic inflammatory cells (when inflammatory cells are scanty the lesion is called gastropathy). The commonest cause of chronic gastritis is Helicobacter pylori, which produces an antral-predominant gastritis with increased acid, whereas autoimmune gastritis is a body- and fundus-restricted atrophic gastritis with parietal cell loss, achlorhydria, hypergastrinaemia, and pernicious anaemia.

Definition and classification. Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa. Acute gastritis (and gastropathy) results from agents that overwhelm mucosal defences (NSAIDs, alcohol, bile, chemotherapy, radiation, ischaemia, stress, uraemia) and shows oedema, congestion, foveolar hyperplasia, neutrophils, and in severe cases erosion and haemorrhage. In the gastrointestinal tract, "acute" refers to the duration of disease rather than to the pattern of inflammation.

Chronic gastritis is caused most commonly by H. pylori
Other causes include NSAIDs, autoimmune gastritis, radiation, chronic bile reflux, mechanical injury, and systemic disease such as Crohn disease, amyloidosis, and graft-versus-host disease. Symptoms of chronic gastritis are milder but more persistent than in acute disease: nausea, upper abdominal pain, and sometimes vomiting, with haematemesis uncommon.

Helicobacter pylori–associated gastritis. H. pylori is a spiral, curved bacillus adapted to the gastric mucus niche. Infection is acquired in childhood by the faecal–oral route, is associated with poverty and crowding, and persists for life without treatment. Virulence depends on flagella (motility in mucus), urease (generates ammonia from urea and raises local pH), adhesins (attachment to foveolar cells), and toxins such as CagA and VacA. Host factors such as pro-inflammatory polymorphisms of TNF and IL-1 and reduced IL-10 influence the outcome.

The infection typically causes a predominantly antral gastritis with normal or increased acid production. Inflammation enhances antral gastrin production, which expands the parietal cell mass and increases acid secretion, predisposing to peptic ulcer. Long-standing infection may extend to the body and fundus (pangastritis), causing patchy atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and reduced acid secretion, which increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.

Histologically, organisms lie in the superficial mucus overlying foveolar cells (best seen with special stains or immunostains). The lamina propria contains numerous plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils, which cross the basement membrane to form pit abscesses. Lymphoid aggregates with germinal centres (induced MALT) are common and may give rise to MALT lymphoma. Diagnosis rests on biopsy, rapid urease test, culture, PCR, urea breath test, stool antigen, or serology
Treatment is a proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics.

Autoimmune gastritis. This accounts for less than 10% of chronic gastritis and is the second or third most frequent cause after H. pylori and NSAIDs. It is an autoimmune attack, mediated by CD4⁺ T cells and antibodies, on the parietal cells of the oxyntic mucosa, with antibodies to H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) and to intrinsic factor. It affects the body and fundus and characteristically spares the antrum.

The loss of parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, which stimulates antral G-cell hyperplasia and marked hypergastrinaemia, and to loss of intrinsic factor with defective ileal absorption of vitamin B₁₂, producing megaloblastic (pernicious) anaemia, atrophic glossitis, and neurologic complications such as subacute combined degeneration. Intestinal metaplasia and endocrine cell hyperplasia are common, and the latter may progress to small multicentric neuroendocrine tumours.

It occurs most often in older women, is associated with other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison disease), and carries an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

An ulcer is a local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. In the stomach the principal ulcers are the chronic peptic ulcer, acute stress ulcers and erosions, drug (NSAID)-induced ulcers, and ulcerating malignancies.

  2. Acute stress-related mucosal ulcers, which are multiple, shallow, and found throughout the stomach in patients with shock, sepsis, severe trauma, or burns (Curling ulcers) or intracranial disease (Cushing ulcers).
  3. Drug-induced ulcers and erosions, notably NSAIDs and aspirin, alcohol, corticosteroids (potentiating NSAIDs), and cytotoxic drugs.
  4. Ulcers of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), which are multiple and may involve the stomach, duodenum, and jejunum.
  5. Malignant ulcers, namely ulcerated gastric adenocarcinoma and occasionally lymphoma.
  6. Rarer lesions: ulcers in granulomatous gastritis (Crohn disease, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), infectious ulcers (CMV, herpes simplex), ischaemic or radiation ulcers, and bleeding from a Dieulafoy lesion (abnormal submucosal artery eroding the mucosa).

Peptic ulcer forms when damaging forces (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm the protective mechanisms of the mucosa, on a background of chronic gastritis. The main complications are haemorrhage, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction, with penetration, intractable pain, and rarely malignant change.

Formation. The gastric mucosa is protected by a mucus–bicarbonate barrier, tight epithelial junctions that limit back-diffusion of acid, rapid epithelial renewal, prostaglandin synthesis, and a rich mucosal blood supply that removes any acid that has diffused into the lamina propria. A peptic ulcer arises when these defences are impaired or the damaging factors are excessive.

H. pylori is the principal cause. The organism lives in the gastric mucus and does not invade the tissues
it injures the mucosa through urease-generated ammonia, CagA and VacA toxins, and the inflammatory response (neutrophils, TNF, IL-1). Antral gastritis increases gastrin and acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion. The acid load produces gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, which becomes colonised and inflamed and finally ulcerates.

NSAIDs cause ulceration by inhibiting COX-dependent prostaglandin synthesis. Smoking reduces mucosal blood flow and healing, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome produces massive acid hypersecretion. Peptic ulcers therefore arise on a background of chronic gastritis.

Complications

  1. Haemorrhage: the most frequent complication (about 15% to 20% of patients)
    Erosion of a thickened vessel in the scarred base (the gastroduodenal artery in posterior duodenal ulcers) causes haematemesis, melaena, or chronic blood loss with iron deficiency anaemia, and it can be life threatening.
  2. Perforation: about 5% of patients, but it accounts for about two-thirds of ulcer-related deaths and is rarely the first indication of an ulcer
    it is commonest with anterior duodenal ulcers and causes peritonitis, with free air under the diaphragm on an upright abdominal radiograph.
  3. Obstruction (about 2%): from oedema or scarring, mostly with pyloric channel and duodenal ulcers, causing incapacitating pain, repeated vomiting, and rarely complete outlet obstruction with metabolic alkalosis.
  4. Penetration into adjacent organs (pancreas, causing back pain; liver) and fistula formation.
  5. Intractable pain and recurrence.
  6. Malignant transformation: rare, and almost exclusively a concern with gastric (not duodenal) ulcers, most of which were malignant from the outset.

A peptic ulcer is usually a solitary, round to oval, sharply punched-out defect with a smooth clean base and radiating folds, and microscopically its base shows four zones: fibrinous debris, neutrophilic exudate, granulation tissue, and fibrous scar.

Gross. More than 80% of peptic ulcers are solitary. They are round to oval, usually less than 3 to 4 cm, with a sharply punched-out appearance. The mucosal margin is usually level with the surrounding mucosa, though it may overhang the base, particularly proximally. heaped-up margins suggest carcinoma. The base is smooth and clean because of peptic digestion of exudate and may be stained brown or black by altered blood.

Scarring may involve the full thickness of the wall and draws the surrounding mucosa into folds that radiate outward like spokes of a wheel. The commonest sites are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curvature of the stomach.

Microscopic. The ulcer extends through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper, and the base has four layers: (1) a thin superficial layer of necrotic fibrinoid debris, often with neutrophils. (2) a zone of active, predominantly neutrophilic inflammation. (3) granulation tissue with immature vessels, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells. and (4) a deep fibrous or collagenous scar that may extend into or through the muscularis propria.

Vessels within the scar are thickened (endarteritis obliterans) and occasionally thrombosed, and eroded vessels account for bleeding. The adjacent mucosa shows chronic gastritis, and foveolar metaplasia is common in duodenal disease, as a protective response.

Helicobacter pylori causes acute and chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease of the stomach and duodenum, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric MALT lymphoma, together with polyps and atrophic changes that link them.

  1. Acute gastritis: usually mild and self-limited, with nonspecific dyspeptic symptoms at the time of infection.
  2. Chronic gastritis: initially a superficial antral gastritis with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils (pit abscesses), and lymphoid follicles with germinal centres. Later a pangastritis.
  3. Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis): patchy, without autoantibodies, with reduced acid output.
  4. Peptic ulcer disease: gastric ulcer and, through increased antral gastrin and acid, duodenal ulcer.
  5. Hyperplastic and inflammatory gastric polyps, which arise in the setting of chronic gastritis and may show dysplasia.
  6. Dysplasia and intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, through the sequence of atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma. The risk is greatest with CagA-positive strains.
  7. Gastric MALT lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma), arising from induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Early tumours without translocation may regress after eradication.
  8. Less commonly, associations with hypertrophic gastropathy (Ménétrier disease), eosinophilic and granulomatous gastritis, and extragastric conditions such as iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

Interestingly, H. pylori infection with atrophy lowers the risk of duodenal ulcer and of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, because of reduced acid secretion.

H. pylori is the commonest identifiable cause of gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type): chronic infection leads through atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma. Linitis plastica is the "leather bottle" stomach produced by diffuse infiltration of the gastric wall by signet-ring cell (diffuse-type) carcinoma, with a desmoplastic reaction, rigidity, and flattening of the rugae.

Role of H. pylori. Most gastric cancers are associated with H. pylori infection, and the decline in gastric cancer incidence in high-income countries has been attributed largely to the decline in infection, chiefly of intestinal-type cancers. The mechanism is the long-standing chronic gastritis that causes multifocal mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, which is the field in which dysplasia and carcinoma arise (the Correa cascade: chronic gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma).

Chronic inflammation exposes the epithelium to free radicals and to regenerative proliferative stimuli, including raised gastrin, which is mitogenic. Achlorhydria permits bacterial overgrowth and production of carcinogenic nitrosamines. Strains carrying the CagA pathogenicity island, present in about 90% of isolates in high-risk populations, colonise the body as well as the antrum and induce cytokine release, atrophy, and metaplasia more effectively.

Host polymorphisms leading to high TNF and IL-1 and low IL-10 increase the risk. In diffuse gastric cancer the pathogenesis involves loss of E-cadherin (CDH1 mutation or promoter hypermethylation). A minority (about 10%) of gastric cancers are instead associated with Epstein–Barr virus. Eradication of H. pylori reduces the risk, and intestinal metaplasia may regress. Infection is also linked to gastric MALT lymphoma. The inverse relationship between duodenal ulcer (high acid) and gastric cancer (atrophy, low acid) is a notable feature.

Linitis plastica. In diffuse-type gastric carcinoma, small clusters and individual discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrate the gastric wall. These cells contain large mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery, and they provoke an intense desmoplastic reaction. Extensive infiltration produces diffuse thickening and rigidity of the stomach wall with flattening of the rugal folds and a contracted lumen, imparting a "leather bottle" appearance, without a discrete mass and often without an ulcer. It carries a very poor prognosis (5-year survival less than 20% in advanced disease).

The principal congenital anomalies of the gastrointestinal tract are atresia, fistulae, and duplications (for example oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula and intestinal atresia), ectopia, Meckel diverticulum, congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and Hirschsprung disease.

  1. Atresia, fistulae, and duplications: failure of canalisation or abnormal septation of the foregut, producing oesophageal atresia (usually with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, causing choking, regurgitation, and aspiration at the first feed), intestinal atresia and stenosis (most frequent in the duodenum), and duplications
    Anorectal malformations (imperforate anus) also belong here.
  2. Ectopia: developmental rests of gastric mucosa (the oesophageal inlet patch) or pancreatic tissue in the oesophagus, stomach, or small intestine. They may cause dysphagia, peptic ulceration, or pyloric obstruction.
  3. Meckel diverticulum: the commonest congenital anomaly of the gut, a true ileal diverticulum from failed involution of the vitelline duct.
  4. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: hyperplasia of the pyloric muscularis presenting at 3 to 6 weeks with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable "olive."
  5. Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): failure of neural crest migration, causing functional distal obstruction.
  6. Others: malrotation and volvulus, abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), and diaphragmatic hernia.

Meckel diverticulum is the commonest congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, a true diverticulum of the ileum caused by failure of involution of the vitelline duct, whereas Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, causing functional obstruction with proximal megacolon.

Meckel diverticulum. A true diverticulum includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which connects the gut lumen to the yolk sac, and arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum. The "rule of 2s" applies: it occurs in about 2% of the population, within about 2 feet (60 cm) of the ileocaecal valve, is about 2 inches (5 cm) long, has a male:female ratio of 2:1, and is most often symptomatic by age 2 (although only about 4% ever become symptomatic).

The lining may resemble normal small intestine, but ectopic gastric (acid-secreting) or pancreatic tissue may be present. The complications are peptic ulceration of the adjacent ileal mucosa with bleeding (occult or massive, particularly in children) and perforation, diverticulitis simulating acute appendicitis, intussusception, volvulus, and obstruction. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan identifies ectopic gastric mucosa.

Hirschsprung disease. Congenital aganglionic megacolon occurs in about 1 in 5000 live births, with a male predominance, and is associated with Down syndrome (about 10%) and other malformations. The enteric neural plexus develops from neural crest cells that migrate into the bowel wall in a craniocaudal direction. When migration is arrested prematurely or ganglion cells die prematurely, the distal segment lacks both Meissner (submucosal) and Auerbach (myenteric) plexuses.

Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RET account for most familial and about 15% of sporadic cases, and mutations in EDNRB and EDN3 have also been implicated. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and is hypercontracted, so peristalsis is absent and functional obstruction results, with dilatation of the proximal normally innervated colon (megacolon). The rectum is always involved. short-segment disease (rectosigmoid) is commoner than long-segment disease.

Diagnosis requires histologic proof of absence of ganglion cells (rectal biopsy; acetylcholinesterase staining highlights hypertrophic nerve fibres). Infants fail to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develop abdominal distention and bilious vomiting. The major risks are enterocolitis, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, perforation, and peritonitis. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with anastomosis of the normal colon to the rectum.

Inflammatory bowel disease comprises two chronic relapsing disorders, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease may involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, is segmental, transmural, and granulomatous, and causes fistulas and strictures, whereas ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, is continuous and limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, and presents with bloody diarrhoea.

Definition and pathogenesis. IBD is a chronic condition composed of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (indeterminate colitis, up to 10% of cases, is the term for those that cannot be classified). It results from a combination of abnormal immune regulation (Th1 and Th17 activation), altered host–microbe interactions (dysbiosis), and epithelial barrier dysfunction in genetically susceptible individuals (NOD2 is the strongest association with Crohn disease
ATG16L1 and IRGM affect autophagy). It most frequently presents in teenage years and the early twenties.

Crohn disease

Macroscopic. Any part of the tract may be involved, most commonly the terminal ileum, ileocaecal valve, and caecum
Small bowel only in about 40%, small bowel and colon in 30%, and colon only in the remainder. The hallmark is skip lesions with sharply delineated diseased segments. Early aphthous ulcers enlarge into deep, linear, serpentine ulcers oriented along the long axis, with oedema, loss of folds, and a cobblestone mucosa.

The wall is thickened, rubbery, and stenotic from transmural inflammation, oedema, fibrosis, and muscular hypertrophy (strictures). Mesenteric fat extends over the serosa ("creeping fat")
Deep fissures lead to abscesses, perforation, and fistulas to other loops, bladder, vagina, or skin.

Microscopic. Transmural inflammation with neutrophilic crypt injury and crypt abscesses, ulceration, crypt distortion, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia, and noncaseating granulomas (in about 35% of cases
a hallmark). Lymphoid aggregates occur throughout the wall.

Clinical. Intermittent diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and fever, with periods of remission. About 20% present acutely with right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis. Blood loss and iron deficiency anaemia (colonic disease)
Protein loss, hypoalbuminaemia, and malabsorption of vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts (small bowel disease). Fibrosing strictures, fistulas, perianal disease
Extraintestinal manifestations (uveitis, migratory polyarthritis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, erythema nodosum, clubbing, primary sclerosing cholangitis). anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies
Smoking is a risk factor
Increased risk of colonic carcinoma with long-standing colonic disease.

Ulcerative colitis

Macroscopic. The rectum is always involved, and disease extends proximally in a continuous manner to variable extent (proctitis, left-sided colitis, pancolitis). The small bowel is spared, apart from mild backwash ileitis in severe pancolitis. The mucosa is red and granular with broad-based ulcers. Islands of regenerating mucosa form pseudopolyps
in chronic disease the mucosa is atrophic and smooth. Because it is not transmural, the wall is not thickened, the serosa is normal, and strictures are not a feature. Severe cases may progress to toxic megacolon with perforation.

Microscopic. Inflammation confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, with a lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic infiltrate, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and atrophy, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia. Granulomas are absent. Sharp demarcation between diseased and normal mucosa may be seen.

Clinical. Relapsing attacks of bloody diarrhoea with stringy mucus, lower abdominal pain, and cramps relieved by defecation. Complications include toxic megacolon, perforation, haemorrhage, and colorectal carcinoma (risk increases sharply 8 to 10 years after onset, and is greatest with pancolitis). Extraintestinal manifestations overlap with Crohn disease, with primary sclerosing cholangitis markedly increased (about 5%)
p-ANCA is positive in about 75%

Carcinoid tumour, now called well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, is a neoplasm of the diffuse neuroendocrine cells of the gut that most often arises in the small intestine, appendix, and rectum and is composed of uniform cells with "salt and pepper" chromatin. Carcinoid syndrome is the constellation of flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis caused by vasoactive substances, mainly serotonin, released into the systemic circulation.

Carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumour. Neuroendocrine tumours arise from the diffuse components of the endocrine system. The term carcinoid is still used in the gut. More than 40% occur in the small intestine
The tracheobronchial tree and lungs are the next commonest site, and the appendix, rectum, and stomach are also important sites. Gastric tumours are associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune atrophic gastritis, MEN1, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. They occur most often in the sixth decade.

Gross. Intramural or submucosal masses forming polypoid nodules with intact or ulcerated overlying mucosa, yellow-tan, and very firm because of intense desmoplasia, which may kink and obstruct the small bowel.

Microscopic. Islands, trabeculae, strands, glands, and sheets of uniform cells with scant pink granular cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei with "salt and pepper" chromatin
Positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin A. Grade is determined by mitotic rate and Ki-67 index. Poorly differentiated tumours are neuroendocrine carcinomas (small cell or large cell).

Behaviour. Prognosis depends on differentiation, mitotic rate, Ki-67, size, and site. Gastric and duodenal tumours rarely metastasise
Jejunal and ileal tumours are often multiple and aggressive. Appendiceal tumours (usually at the tip, less than 2 cm) are almost always benign. Rectal tumours are usually small and rarely metastasise.

Carcinoid syndrome. It develops in fewer than 10% of patients, and is caused by vasoactive substances (serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, tachykinins) secreted by the tumour into the systemic circulation. It occurs when the tumour products bypass the first-pass metabolism by the liver, so it is strongly associated with hepatic metastases (or tumours draining into a nonportal venous bed, such as bronchial carcinoids).

The clinical diagnosis is acute appendicitis. It is confirmed by clinical scoring and imaging (ultrasound or computed tomography), and ultimately by histological examination of the removed appendix, which shows neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria.

Diagnosis. Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency of adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance. The picture here is classic: periumbilical pain that localises to the right iliac fossa (McBurney point), nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, localised tenderness with rebound (peritoneal irritation), and neutrophilic leucocytosis. It is thought to be initiated by increased intraluminal pressure with compromised venous outflow, most often following luminal obstruction (in 50% to 80% of cases) by a faecalith, or less commonly by a gallstone, tumour, worms (Enterobius), or by lymphoid hyperplasia, with bacterial proliferation, ischaemia, and inflammation.

  3. Imaging: graded-compression ultrasonography (noncompressible, blind-ending tubular structure more than 6 mm in diameter) in children and young patients, and contrast-enhanced computed tomography when needed. Plain abdominal radiography may show a faecalith.
  4. Diagnostic laparoscopy when doubt persists, which can proceed directly to appendectomy.
  5. Definitive confirmation: histopathology of the appendectomy specimen (neutrophils in the muscularis propria).

Cirrhosis is a diffuse, irreversible-in-its-established-form process of the liver in which fibrosis and the conversion of normal liver architecture into regenerative parenchymal nodules, surrounded by fibrous bands, is accompanied by vascular remodeling and shunting. It is classified by morphology into micronodular, macronodular, and mixed types, and by aetiology.

Definition. Cirrhosis is a diffuse remodeling of the entire liver into parenchymal nodules (often regenerative) surrounded by fibrous bands, with a variable degree of vascular (often portosystemic) shunting. It is the end stage of many chronic liver diseases. The three hallmarks are diffuse involvement, bridging fibrous septa, and regenerative nodules, with disruption of the lobular architecture.

It is not a specific diagnosis, and cirrhosis and liver failure are not synonymous: some cirrhotic patients, such as those whose hepatitis B is suppressed or whose hepatitis C is cured, may never progress to end-stage disease.

Types

  1. Morphological classification (by nodule size):
    • Micronodular cirrhosis: nodules uniformly less than 3 mm
      Typical of alcohol-associated cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis), haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction, and hepatic venous outflow obstruction.
    • Macronodular cirrhosis: nodules larger than 3 mm (up to several centimetres), typical of post-necrotic or post-viral hepatitis cirrhosis, Wilson disease, and α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.
    • Mixed (micro-macronodular) cirrhosis.
  2. Aetiological classification: alcoholic, post-viral (post-necrotic), biliary (primary and secondary), cardiac (congestive), metabolic and inherited (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), steatohepatitic (MASH), autoimmune, drug-induced, and cryptogenic (more than 90% of "cryptogenic" cirrhosis is probably burned-out MASH).
  3. Functional classification: compensated and decompensated cirrhosis.
69:
The leading causes of cirrhosis worldwide are chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, with biliary diseases, autoimmune hepatitis, and inherited metabolic disorders as other causes.

  1. Chronic viral hepatitis: hepatitis B (with or without D) and hepatitis C.
  2. Alcohol-associated liver disease (micronodular, Laennec).
  3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), the commonest cause in many Western countries, accounting for most "cryptogenic" cirrhosis.
  4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (secondary biliary cirrhosis), biliary atresia, and cystic fibrosis.
  5. Autoimmune hepatitis.
  6. Inherited and metabolic disorders: hereditary haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, glycogen storage diseases.
  7. Vascular causes: chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Budd–Chiari syndrome), chronic right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis).
  8. Drugs and toxins: methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid, and others.
  9. Chronic parasitic disease: schistosomiasis (periportal fibrosis).
  10. Cryptogenic cirrhosis: no cause identified.

The likely diagnosis is decompensated cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension, most probably alcohol-associated. Gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy reflect hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism from impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogen, and the liver function tests that are altered are bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, globulins, and prothrombin time.

Diagnosis. A middle-aged man with jaundice (hepatic failure), gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy (impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, leading to hyperoestrogenaemia, and hypogonadism), and ascites (portal hypertension with hypoalbuminaemia) has cirrhosis of the liver in a decompensated stage. Other expected findings are palmar erythema, spider angiomas, loss of body hair, caput medusae, splenomegaly, variceal haemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy.

The commonest cause in such a patient is alcohol, and chronic hepatitis B or C and MASH must be considered. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography, elastography, endoscopy for varices, and liver biopsy where indicated, and by testing for the cause.

Liver function tests altered

  • Serum bilirubin raised (mixed hyperbilirubinaemia).
  • AST and ALT mildly to moderately raised (AST > ALT, ratio 2:1 or more in alcoholic cirrhosis).
  • Alkaline phosphatase (and GGT) variably raised.
  • Serum albumin reduced, with raised globulins (reversed A:G ratio).
  • Prothrombin time prolonged (reduced synthesis of clotting factors).
  • Others: raised serum ammonia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism).

Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid in the peritoneal cavity. It is a transudate in most hepatic and cardiac causes and an exudate in infective or malignant causes, and the commonest cause overall is cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension.

Definition. Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, clinically detectable when at least about 500 mL has accumulated (shifting dullness, fluid thrill). In 85% of cases it is caused by cirrhosis. Cirrhotic ascites is serous with a low protein content (less than 3 g/dL) and a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more
The fluid may contain scant mesothelial cells and mononuclear cells, neutrophils suggest infection, and red cells suggest disseminated intra-abdominal cancer.

The overwhelming majority of gallbladder carcinomas are adenocarcinomas, usually arising in the fundus on a background of chronic cholecystitis with gallstones.

Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the commonest malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. The tumours are mainly adenocarcinomas, growing either as a firm, poorly circumscribed mass or as a diffuse infiltration of the gallbladder wall that simulates chronic cholecystitis. They are most often found in the fundus. Microscopically they consist of glands (of intestinal, biliary, or papillary pattern, and occasionally mucinous or signet-ring) in a desmoplastic stroma. in some, cytologic atypia and stromal response are minimal and perineural and vascular invasion help to establish the diagnosis. Rarely, other primary tumours occur, such as neuroendocrine tumours, squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and sarcomas.

The precursor lesions are flat dysplasia (carcinoma in situ), intracholecystic papillary-tubular neoplasms, and intestinal metaplasia. Gallstones are present in 95% of cases, with chronic inflammation the common thread. Other risk factors are female sex (at least twice as common), porcelain gallbladder and hyalinising cholecystitis, chronic Salmonella typhi carriage, anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, and, in high-incidence areas (Chile, Bolivia, northern India, and Native American populations), ethnicity. Molecular changes include TP53 mutations and alterations of the EGFR family (HER2) and RAS.

The tumour is diagnosed late (preoperative diagnosis in under 20%), spreading by direct extension into the liver and adjacent organs, along the peritoneum and biliary tree, and by metastasis to the liver and portahepatic nodes. The 5-year survival is less than 10%, but incidental carcinoma found early at cholecystectomy can be cured by resection.

Nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation, characterised by haematuria with red cell casts, oliguria with azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension, whereas nephrotic syndrome is due to increased glomerular permeability and is characterised by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Microscopically, nephritic syndrome shows red cells and red cell casts in the urine and hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli, while nephrotic syndrome shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts in the urine and normal or only thickened glomeruli with podocyte foot process effacement. Serum complement is usually low in nephritic syndrome of the postinfectious type and normal in the common causes of nephrotic syndrome.

Complete explanation

Nephritic syndrome results from proliferative, inflammatory glomerular disease. The cellular proliferation and leucocyte infiltration injure the capillary wall, allowing blood into the urine, and reduce GFR, leading to oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention and hypertension. The classic example is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Others are rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy and proliferative lupus nephritis.

Nephrotic syndrome results from a derangement of the glomerular filter, structural or charge-related, that permits plasma proteins to leak. There is typically little inflammation.

Glomerulonephritis is a group of diseases, mostly immunologically mediated, in which the glomeruli are the primary site of injury, usually with proliferation of glomerular cells and an inflammatory reaction. The five main primary glomerular diseases are acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy complete the list.

Complete explanation

Glomerulonephritis denotes inflammatory disease of the glomerulus, most often caused by immunologic mechanisms: deposition or in situ formation of immune complexes, antibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane, or cell-mediated immunity. Because some of the glomerular diseases have no cellular inflammatory component (minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, for example), the term glomerulopathy is used for them.

Diseases in which the kidney is the sole or predominant organ affected are called primary
Those that are a manifestation of systemic disease, such as lupus, diabetes, amyloidosis or vasculitis, are secondary.

The primary glomerular diseases are:

  1. Acute postinfectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome
  2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of function
  3. Membranous nephropathy — nephrotic syndrome
  4. Minimal change disease — nephrotic syndrome, the commonest cause in children
  5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — nephrotic syndrome and progressive disease
  6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and C3 glomerulopathies — mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture
  7. IgA nephropathy — recurrent haematuria, the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide
79:
Nephritic syndrome is the clinical presentation of inflammatory glomerular disease, with haematuria and red cell casts, oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension. Its complications include acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia and uraemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema, progression to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and eventually chronic kidney disease.

Complete explanation

The syndrome arises when proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli injures the capillary walls and reduces the glomerular filtration rate. Because of reduced filtration, salt and water are retained and nitrogenous waste accumulates. Hypertension arises from the volume expansion and from renin release by the ischaemic kidneys.

Complications in the acute phase follow directly from these disturbances:

  • Acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria, azotaemia and uraemia, accompanied by hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy, with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
  • Circulatory overload, with acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema.
  • Heavy proteinuria, occasionally reaching nephrotic range.

Complications in the later course

  • Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, with extensive crescent formation and rapid loss of renal function over weeks. This is the most serious sequel and may follow postinfectious glomerulonephritis in a small minority of children and more often in adults.
  • Chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease, which may end in end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. Persistent proteinuria and an abnormal GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis.
78:
Acute glomerulonephritis is an acute nephritic syndrome caused by inflammatory proliferation of glomerular cells, of which acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the prototype. It is an immune complex disease: after a pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A β-haemolytic streptococcus, streptococcal antigen, notably pyogenic exotoxin B, and its antibody form immune complexes in the glomerular capillary wall, activate complement, attract neutrophils and monocytes, and cause proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, reducing the glomerular filtration rate.

Complete explanation

Definition. Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a clinical syndrome of acute onset with haematuria, oliguria, azotaemia, mild proteinuria, hypertension and periorbital oedema, caused by diffuse proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli. In its classic form it appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection, mainly in children aged 6 to 10 years.

Role of streptococcal infection in pathogenesis

  1. Nephritogenic strains. Only particular strains of group A β-haemolytic streptococci cause nephritis. Over 90% of cases are linked to M types 1, 4 and 12, which are typed by their cell wall M protein.
  2. Antigen–antibody complexes. Streptococcal antigen, most importantly streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B, is first planted in subendothelial sites in the capillary wall, where it forms immune complexes in situ with antibody. The complexes then dissociate, cross the basement membrane and re-form on the subepithelial side, appearing as humps. Circulating complexes may contribute.
  3. Latent period. The interval of 1 to 4 weeks matches the time required for antibody production and immune complex formation.
  4. Complement activation and inflammation. The complexes activate complement
    C5a and other mediators attract neutrophils and monocytes, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, producing hypercellular glomeruli that obliterate the capillary lumens.
  5. Functional result. GFR falls, causing oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention, oedema and hypertension. Damage to the capillary wall allows haematuria and mild proteinuria.

Evidence of an immunological basis. The latent period, elevated antistreptococcal antibody titers, low serum C3 from complement consumption, and granular immunofluorescent deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli, with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, all point to an immune complex mechanism.
80:
The clinical diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The urine is expected to show red blood cells, many of them dysmorphic, together with red cell casts, along with mild proteinuria, white cells, and granular and hyaline casts.

Complete explanation

The age of the child, the periorbital oedema, the high-coloured (smoky) scanty urine and the history of a sore throat about two weeks earlier fit acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period corresponds to the time needed for antibodies to form against nephritogenic streptococcal antigens and for immune complexes to deposit in the glomeruli, causing inflammation. Oliguria and oedema reflect the reduced glomerular filtration rate and salt and water retention, and the coloured urine reflects haematuria.

Expected microscopic urine findings

  • Numerous red cells, many dysmorphic (acanthocytes), reflecting passage through damaged glomerular capillaries.
  • Red cell casts, indicating glomerular origin of the bleeding.
  • Granular and hyaline casts, a few white cells and tubular epithelial cells.
  • Mild to moderate proteinuria (usually less than 1 g/day) on chemical testing.

Supporting tests are a raised antistreptolysin O titer, a low serum C3, and a raised serum urea and creatinine.

Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis, most often due to ascending bacterial infection from the lower urinary tract. It is predisposed to by urinary tract obstruction and stasis, vesicoureteral reflux, instrumentation or catheterisation, pregnancy, female sex, diabetes mellitus, preexisting renal lesions, and immunosuppression.

Complete explanation

Pyelonephritis is one of the commonest diseases of the kidney. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation, usually bacterial, associated with urinary tract infection. Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring involving the calyces and pelvis, which results from recurrent episodes of infection in the presence of predisposing factors such as reflux and obstruction.

More than 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, above all Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. The kidney is reached either by the ascending route from the bladder (the commoner route) or by the bloodstream (as in infective endocarditis or in debilitated or obstructed patients).

Predisposing factors

  • Urinary tract obstruction and stasis, whether congenital or acquired (stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, neurogenic bladder), because residual urine allows bacteria to multiply unhindered.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux, which carry infected bladder urine into the renal pelvis and parenchyma.
  • Instrumentation of the urinary tract, particularly catheterisation, and cystoscopy.
  • Pregnancy, in which 4% to 6% of women develop bacteriuria and 20% to 40% of these develop symptomatic infection if untreated.
  • Sex and age: infections are much more frequent in females up to about 40 years of age
    in older males the incidence rises because of prostatic enlargement and instrumentation. Congenital anomalies are important in infant boys.
  • Diabetes mellitus, through increased susceptibility to infection, neurogenic bladder and frequent instrumentation.
  • Immunosuppression and immunodeficiency, and preexisting renal lesions with scarring and obstruction.
84:
Urinary tract infection is infection of any part of the urinary tract by microorganisms, usually bacteria, shown by significant bacteriuria and pyuria. it may involve the bladder (cystitis) or the kidney (pyelonephritis). It is most common in females, because of the short urethra and other anatomical and hormonal factors, and also in infants with congenital anomalies, elderly men with prostatic enlargement, pregnant women, diabetics, and patients with obstruction, stones, catheters or immunosuppression.

Complete explanation

Urinary tract infection (UTI) is characterised by bacteriuria and pyuria, the presence of bacteria and leucocytes in the urine. It may be symptomatic or asymptomatic and may involve the lower tract (urethritis, cystitis, prostatitis) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis). By convention a count of 10⁵ or more organisms per mL in a properly collected midstream sample is taken as significant. Over 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, most commonly E. coli.

Who is commonly affected, and why

  • Females. After the first year of life and up to about 40 years of age, infection is much commoner in women. The reasons are the shorter female urethra, the close proximity of the urethral meatus to the anus and vagina, the absence of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid, hormonal changes that affect bacterial adherence to the mucosa, and urethral trauma during sexual intercourse.
  • Pregnant women, because of ureteric dilatation and stasis, with a risk of progression of asymptomatic bacteriuria to pyelonephritis.
  • Infants and young boys with congenital anomalies, such as obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux.
  • Older men, in whom prostatic hypertrophy causes obstruction and incomplete emptying, and in whom instrumentation is frequent.
  • Diabetics, who have increased susceptibility to infection and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
  • Patients with obstruction, stones, neurogenic bladder, catheters or instrumentation, and those who are immunosuppressed.
86:
The probable diagnosis is acute urinary tract infection, most likely acute cystitis with ascending involvement of the kidney, that is acute pyelonephritis, since fever accompanies the dysuria. It is investigated by urine routine examination and microscopy, midstream urine culture and sensitivity, a complete blood count, serum creatinine, and imaging of the urinary tract.

Complete explanation

Dysuria and difficulty with micturition indicate irritation of the bladder and urethra (cystitis and urethritis) in a young woman, in whom the shorter urethra predisposes to ascending infection by enteric bacteria, chiefly E. coli. Fever of five days' duration suggests spread to the upper tract and acute pyelonephritis, which is also suggested if there is loin pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

Investigations

  1. Urine examination. The urine contains many leucocytes (pyuria) and bacteria. Microscopy may show leucocyte casts, which indicate renal involvement because casts form only in the tubules. A dipstick may show a positive leucocyte esterase and nitrite test, and there may be microscopic haematuria.
  2. Urine culture and sensitivity on a clean-catch midstream specimen, the definitive diagnostic test, showing significant growth (10⁵ or more organisms/mL) of the causative organism and guiding antibiotic therapy.
  3. Blood tests: complete blood count (neutrophil leucocytosis), ESR/CRP, serum urea and creatinine. Blood culture if there is high fever or suspected septicaemia.
  4. Imaging. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder to detect obstruction, stones and residual urine. Further imaging (CT, intravenous urography, voiding cystourethrography) if infection is recurrent or complicated, to look for reflux, obstruction or scarring.
  5. A pregnancy test should be done before imaging or treatment in a woman of this age.

The four common types of renal calculi are calcium stones (calcium oxalate with or without calcium phosphate), the commonest at about 70%
Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones, formed after infection by urea-splitting bacteria. Uric acid stones
and cystine stones. A single common diagnostic test is a plain X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, which shows radiopaque stones.

Complete explanation

Urolithiasis affects 5% to 10% of people during their lifetime, more often males, with peak onset between 20 and 30 years. The most important determinant of stone formation is a raised urinary concentration of the stone constituents that exceeds their solubility (supersaturation). Low urine volume, altered urinary pH, infection, and deficiency of crystal inhibitors (citrate, pyrophosphate, osteopontin, nephrocalcin) contribute.

  1. Calcium stones (about 70%) — calcium oxalate or calcium oxalate mixed with calcium phosphate. Most are associated with hypercalciuria, with or without hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, bone disease), and some with hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria or hypocitraturia. They are radiopaque.
  2. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones (5–10%) — formed in alkaline urine after infection with urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus. They can grow into large staghorn calculi that cast the pelvicalyceal system.
  3. Uric acid stones (5–10%) — occur in gout, leukaemia and other hyperuricaemic states, but over half of patients have no hyperuricaemia, only persistently acid urine (pH below 5.5). They are radiolucent.
  4. Cystine stones (1–2%) — caused by inherited defects in tubular reabsorption of amino acids (cystinuria), forming in acid urine.

An organic mucoprotein matrix, forming 1% to 5% of the stone by weight, is present in all calculi.

Diagnosis. Plain radiography of the abdomen (KUB) is the commonest single test because most stones (calcium and struvite) are radiopaque. Ultrasonography and non-contrast CT are alternatives, CT being the most sensitive, and uric acid stones, being radiolucent, may be missed on plain films. Urinalysis shows haematuria and crystals.

Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine, either grossly visible or detected only on microscopy. Renal causes include glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, renal calculi and renal tumours such as renal cell carcinoma. post-renal causes include ureteric or bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostate carcinoma.

Complete explanation

Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of the normal, conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field in a centrifuged specimen. It is gross (macroscopic) when the urine is visibly red, smoky or cola-coloured, and microscopic when blood is detected only by dipstick or microscopy. It is one of the commonest manifestations of renal and urinary tract disease and, when painless, must always be investigated to exclude a neoplasm.

Renal causes (any four of the following)

  1. Glomerulonephritis — acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, crescentic glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome
  2. Acute pyelonephritis, and renal tuberculosis
  3. Renal calculi
  4. Renal tumours — renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour, urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
  5. Polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney
  6. Renal trauma, papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse), renal infarction, and vascular malformations

Post-renal causes (any four of the following)

The important renal function tests are those of glomerular function — serum creatinine, blood urea, creatinine clearance and estimated GFR — and of tubular function, such as urine concentration, together with urinalysis for protein and sediment. Serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea because creatinine is produced at a constant rate from muscle, is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, and is largely unaffected by diet, hydration or liver function, whereas urea varies with all of these.

Complete explanation

Important renal function tests

  1. Glomerular filtration: serum creatinine and blood urea (BUN)
    Creatinine clearance
    Estimated GFR (derived from serum creatinine, age and sex). Cystatin C
    Inulin clearance (the reference method, used for research).
  2. Tubular function: urine specific gravity and osmolality, the concentration test after water deprivation, urinary acidification, and tests for specific tubular transport defects.
  3. Urinalysis: protein, albumin–creatinine ratio, and microscopy for red cells, casts and crystals.
  4. Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate) and acid–base status. and imaging.

Why serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea

  • Creatinine is produced from muscle creatine at a steady rate proportional to muscle mass, so its plasma level is stable. it is freely filtered at the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, with only slight tubular secretion. Its level therefore reflects GFR.
  • Urea production varies widely: it increases with high protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, catabolic states, tissue breakdown, fever and corticosteroids, and falls in liver disease and low protein intake. A large fraction of filtered urea is passively reabsorbed in the tubules, and this increases in dehydration and reduced flow, so blood urea rises in prerenal states without any parenchymal damage.
  • Creatinine is thus a more reliable index of GFR, although it is insensitive in early disease, since it rises above normal only after GFR has fallen by about half.

Bence Jones protein is free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) excreted in the urine. Because the light chains are small, they are filtered by the glomerulus. It is found chiefly in multiple myeloma, and also in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, light-chain amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease and other plasma cell disorders. It is detected by urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, and classically by the heat test.

Complete explanation

What it is. Bence Jones protein consists of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, produced in excess by a neoplastic clone of plasma cells, which are small enough to be filtered at the glomerulus and appear in the urine. The reagent strip, which detects mainly albumin, may be negative, though the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive.

Conditions in which it is found

  1. Multiple myeloma (the commonest), with Bence Jones proteinuria detectable in a large proportion of patients
  2. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and other lymphoplasmacytic disorders
  3. AL amyloidosis (primary amyloidosis), in which the light chains form amyloid, and light-chain deposition disease
  4. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and occasionally chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphomas

Renal significance. In myeloma, Bence Jones proteins injure the kidney in two ways: some light chains are directly toxic to tubular epithelial cells, and others combine with Tamm–Horsfall protein under acidic conditions to form large tubular casts that obstruct the tubules and provoke a giant cell reaction (light-chain cast nephropathy, "myeloma kidney"). This is the main cause of renal dysfunction in myeloma, which develops in about half the patients. Light chains also cause AL amyloidosis and light-chain deposition disease.

Laboratory detection

  1. Heat test (classic). On slow heating of acidified urine (pH about 5), the protein precipitates at 40–60 °C, redissolves partially or completely on boiling at about 100 °C, and reappears on cooling. The test is now of historical interest because it is insensitive and unreliable.
  2. Urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation. The definitive method, performed on a concentrated 24-hour urine specimen, which shows a monoclonal band and identifies its type (kappa or lambda).
  3. Serum free light-chain assay and serum protein electrophoresis, which are more sensitive.
  4. Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells.

PSA, prostate-specific antigen, is a serine protease produced by the prostatic epithelium and normally secreted in semen, where it liquefies the seminal coagulum. Only minute amounts circulate in normal serum. Its clinical importance is in the detection, staging and especially the follow-up of prostate cancer, although it is organ specific rather than cancer specific, and is also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, infarction, and after instrumentation.

Complete explanation

PSA is an androgen-regulated serine protease secreted by prostatic epithelium whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation. In healthy men only minute amounts are found in the serum.

Clinical importance

  1. Detection and diagnosis. Elevated blood levels occur in both localised and advanced prostate cancer, and PSA is widely used with digital rectal examination to select patients for biopsy.
  2. Monitoring after treatment. Once the diagnosis has been established, serial measurement after therapy is of clear value in monitoring recurrence and disease progression.
  3. Prognosis and staging, in combination with grade and stage.

Limitations. PSA is organ specific, but not cancer specific. Serum levels are on average lower in benign prostatic hyperplasia than in cancer, but the two overlap considerably. Prostatitis, prostatic infarction, instrumentation of the prostate and ejaculation also increase PSA. Its sensitivity and specificity as a screening test are suboptimal: false-negative results occur, and many cancers are indolent, so that screening leads to overdiagnosis and overtreatment, for which reason some countries do not recommend its use for screening.
