SF-1 for gonadotroph tumours). Histologically they are soft, circumscribed, composed of monotonous polygonal cells in sheets or cords with a sparse reticulin network, which distinguishes them from the mixed cell population and rich reticulin of normal anterior pituitary.

The lactotroph tumour is the most common functioning PitNET. Hyperprolactinaemia produces amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido and infertility, and is detected earlier in females than in males. Serum prolactin tends to rise in proportion to tumour size. Hyperprolactinaemia is not always due to a tumour: it also occurs in pregnancy, with dopamine-blocking drugs, with hypothyroidism and renal failure, and when any suprasellar mass interrupts the dopaminergic inhibition travelling down the pituitary stalk. Treatment is usually with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine or cabergoline).

The somatotroph tumour secretes growth hormone, which stimulates hepatic IGF-1. In children before epiphyseal closure it causes gigantism. in adults it causes acromegaly, with enlargement of the jaw, hands, feet and viscera, together with glucose intolerance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy. These tumours are often large at diagnosis because the clinical changes are insidious.

Any PitNET may cause mass effects: erosion of the sella turcica, compression of the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia), headache, hypopituitarism through destruction of normal gland, and pituitary apoplexy after haemorrhage into the tumour. A corticotroph tumour causes Cushing disease.
99:
Two benign thyroid tumours are follicular adenoma and oncocytic (Hürthle cell) adenoma. The four main malignant tumours are papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma is the most common, accounting for about 85% of thyroid cancers, and has an excellent prognosis with a 10-year survival above 95%.

Complete explanation: Follicular adenoma is a solitary, encapsulated nodule of well-differentiated follicles that compresses adjacent gland. it is diagnosed only after the capsule has been examined and found to lack invasion. A minority are functioning (toxic adenoma).

Among the malignant tumours, papillary carcinoma arises in young and middle-aged adults and spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes. Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood. Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells, about 70% sporadic and the rest in MEN-2 with germline RET mutations. Anaplastic carcinoma arises in the elderly, often from a pre-existing differentiated tumour, and is almost uniformly fatal within a year.

Prognosis of papillary carcinoma is influenced by age (worse above 55), extrathyroidal extension and distant metastasis. Local recurrence occurs in 5–20% and distant spread in 10–15%.
100:
Follicular adenoma is a benign, encapsulated thyroid tumour of well-differentiated follicular cells, whereas follicular carcinoma is the malignant counterpart that shows capsular and/or vascular invasion. FNAC cannot separate them, because the cytology is identical. The distinction needs histological examination of the entire capsule.

Complete explanation: Both tumours are composed of uniform follicles containing colloid, and both commonly harbour RAS mutations. Cytologically, an aspirate from either shows cellular smears of follicular cells in microfollicles without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. The decisive feature of carcinoma is invasion: penetration of the tumour capsule, invasion of vessels within or beyond the capsule (usually veins), or invasion of adjacent thyroid.

Because this can be assessed only by extensive sampling of the capsule in the resected specimen, FNAC results are reported as "follicular neoplasm" and the nodule is surgically excised (lobectomy), with molecular testing sometimes helping to stratify indeterminate nodules. Adenomas do not recur or metastasise
Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone, lung and liver.
101:
Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormone due to overactivity of the thyroid gland. Strictly, thyrotoxicosis is the broader term and includes causes in which hormone excess does not arise from gland hyperfunction. The commonest cause is Graves disease.

Complete explanation: Types are as follows.

Associated with increased gland function (true hyperthyroidism):

  • Primary: Graves disease (diffuse hyperplasia, about 85% of cases), toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease), toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis from maternal Graves disease.
  • Secondary: TSH-secreting pituitary tumour (rare)
    Here TSH is normal or raised.

Thyrotoxicosis without increased gland function: granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless thyroiditis, struma ovarii and factitious thyrotoxicosis from exogenous thyroxine.

In all except the pituitary type, TSH is suppressed. The clinical effects are heat intolerance, weight loss with increased appetite, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, proximal myopathy, diarrhoea and osteoporosis, with a staring gaze and lid lag from sympathetic overactivity. Radioiodine uptake distinguishes diffuse increased uptake (Graves), a hot nodule (toxic adenoma) and low uptake (thyroiditis).
102:
A young woman with a diffusely enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos has Graves disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Her thyroid hormone status will show raised free T₄ and T₃ with suppressed TSH. Hypothyroidism is the opposite state of thyroid hormone deficiency, caused most often by Hashimoto thyroiditis, iodine deficiency and iatrogenic ablation.

Complete explanation: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that stimulate the TSH receptor. Free T₄ and T₃ are elevated and TSH is suppressed. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased and TSI/TRAb are present. The gland shows diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the epithelium with lymphoid infiltrates.

Hypothyroidism is a state of structural or functional derangement that interferes with thyroid hormone production. It is classified as primary (intrinsic thyroid disease), secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic). Common causes are Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common in iodine-sufficient regions), endemic iodine deficiency, surgical or radioiodine ablation, drugs (lithium, amiodarone, thionamides), congenital biosynthetic defects and thyroid dysgenesis.

Serum TSH is raised in primary disease and is the most sensitive screening test. In infancy, deficiency produces cretinism with intellectual disability. in adults it causes myxoedema with slowing of mental and physical activity, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, non-pitting oedema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and hypercholesterolaemia.
103:
Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It is classified by pattern into diffuse and multinodular, and by function into non-toxic (euthyroid or hypothyroid) and toxic (hyperthyroid).

Complete explanation

  1. Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goitre: the whole gland is enlarged without nodules. It is endemic (iodine deficiency, goitrogens) or sporadic (goitrogenic drugs, dyshormonogenesis, usually unknown cause). It evolves from a hyperplastic phase to a colloid involution phase.
  2. Multinodular goitre: irregular nodular enlargement resulting from recurrent hyperplasia and involution. Usually euthyroid, but occasionally toxic (Plummer disease).
  3. Diffuse toxic goitre: Graves disease.
  4. Goitrous thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis with goitre.
  5. Neoplastic enlargement from a tumour.

The common mechanism is raised TSH from reduced hormone output, producing hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the follicular epithelium. in most patients the enlarged functional mass restores euthyroidism, and only when the defect is severe does goitrous hypothyroidism result. Clinical features arise mainly from mass effect.
105:
Hypoglycaemia is a fall in blood glucose to a level low enough to cause symptoms of neuroglycopenia and adrenergic activation, generally below about 3.0 mmol/L (50–54 mg/dL). In the acute situation hypoglycaemia is the more immediately dangerous, because the brain depends on a continuous glucose supply and prolonged hypoglycaemia causes irreversible neuronal injury and death within hours. Hyperglycaemia is dangerous mainly through chronic complications, although severe acute hyperglycaemia (ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state) is also life-threatening.

Complete explanation: The brain accounts for about 20% of the body's oxygen consumption and is strictly dependent on aerobic glucose metabolism, so the cellular effects of glucose deprivation resemble those of hypoxia. The cortical pyramidal neurons, the CA1 (Sommer) sector of the hippocampus and the cerebellar Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable. Clinically, hypoglycaemia presents with dizziness, confusion, sweating, palpitations and tachycardia, progressing to loss of consciousness and coma.

It most often complicates insulin or sulfonylurea therapy (missed meals, excess exercise, over-dosage), and also occurs with insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency and severe liver disease. Patients with long-standing frequent episodes may lose warning symptoms ("hypoglycaemia unawareness"), so that neurological impairment is the first sign. Rapid correction with oral or intravenous glucose prevents permanent damage.

Chronic hyperglycaemia, by contrast, damages vessels and nerves slowly over 15 to 20 years, causing nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and accelerated atherosclerosis.
106:
Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is haemoglobin A to which glucose has become non-enzymatically attached. Its level reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding two to three months, so it is the standard measure of long-term glycaemic control and is also used to diagnose diabetes.

Complete explanation: Glucose combines non-enzymatically and irreversibly with the amino terminal valine of the β-chain of HbA, and the amount formed is proportional to the prevailing glucose concentration over the life span of the red cell (about 120 days), weighted towards the most recent weeks. It is not affected by day-to-day fluctuations or by fasting. A value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic of diabetes, 5.7–6.4% indicates prediabetes, and in most diabetic patients the treatment target is below 7%.

Higher values correlate with a greater risk of microvascular complications. Results are unreliable in conditions altering red cell survival or haemoglobin structure (haemolytic anaemia, recent haemorrhage or transfusion, haemoglobinopathies, iron deficiency, chronic renal failure).
107:
A diabetic who becomes unconscious after a chest infection, omits insulin or antidiabetic treatment and has a fruity or musty odour on the breath has diabetic ketoacidosis. Urine analysis will show marked glycosuria and ketonuria.

Complete explanation: Infection raises counter-regulatory hormones (epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol) that block insulin action while insulin is absent or insufficient. The combination of insulin deficiency and glucagon excess increases gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted to ketone bodies (acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid, with acetone, which causes the odour).

Hyperglycaemia (usually 250–600 mg/dL) causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration
Ketone accumulation causes metabolic acidosis with deep, laboured (Kussmaul) breathing, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and eventually coma. In the urine one finds heavy glycosuria, positive ketones on nitroprusside testing, an acid reaction and a high specific gravity. Protein and pus cells may be present if there is renal involvement or infection.

Blood shows high glucose, ketonaemia, low bicarbonate and pH, raised anion gap, and a total body potassium deficit even though serum potassium may be initially raised.
108:
The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) measures the body's ability to dispose of a standard oral glucose load. After a 75 g glucose load in an adult, a two-hour plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more establishes diabetes, whereas 7.8–11.0 mmol/L defines impaired glucose tolerance. Renal glycosuria is glucose in urine despite normal blood glucose because of a low renal threshold, and alimentary glycosuria is transient glycosuria after a meal due to rapid absorption.

Complete explanation

Procedure. The patient eats an unrestricted, carbohydrate-adequate diet (at least 150 g daily) for three days and remains physically active, and fasts for 8–14 hours overnight with no smoking or exercise. A fasting blood sample is taken. The patient drinks 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in about 250–300 mL water within five minutes (1.75 g/kg up to 75 g in children). A further sample is taken at two hours, with additional samples at 30-minute intervals when a curve is wanted. Urine may be tested at each interval.

Indications. Borderline fasting glucose (impaired fasting glucose)
Suspected diabetes with a normal fasting value
Screening for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks
Unexplained glycosuria
Unexplained neuropathy, retinopathy or nephropathy. and assessment of high-risk individuals such as the obese and those with a family history.

Interpretation.

Renal glycosuria: the renal tubular threshold (about 10 mmol/L or 180 mg/dL) is abnormally low (familial, pregnancy, tubular disease), so glucose appears in urine although the OGTT curve is normal.

Alimentary (lag-storage) glycosuria: rapid absorption after gastrectomy, gastroenterostomy or thyrotoxicosis produces a high early peak above the renal threshold with glycosuria, but fasting and 2-hour values are normal.
109:
Diabetes mellitus is classified by pathogenesis into type 1, type 2, other specific types and gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy.

Complete explanation

  1. Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β-cell destruction leading to absolute insulin deficiency (5–10% of cases).
  2. Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance with inadequate β-cell compensation (90–95%).
  3. Other specific types:
    • Monogenic β-cell defects: maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY, HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK and others), neonatal diabetes (KCNJ11, ABCC8), maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (mitochondrial DNA), insulin gene mutations.
    • Genetic defects of insulin action (insulin receptor mutations, type A insulin resistance).
    • Exocrine pancreatic disease ("type 3c"): chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy or trauma, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis.
    • Endocrinopathies: Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, glucagonoma, hyperthyroidism.
    • Drug- or chemical-induced: glucocorticoids, thiazides, nicotinic acid, phenytoin, β-adrenergic agonists.
    • Infections (congenital rubella, cytomegalovirus) and genetic syndromes (Down, Turner, Klinefelter).
  4. Gestational diabetes mellitus: glucose intolerance first detected in pregnancy, which occurs because pregnancy is a diabetogenic state. it usually resolves after delivery but most affected women develop overt diabetes within 10 to 20 years.
110:
The ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone. Ketonuria occurs whenever fat is being oxidised faster than the tissues can use the ketones formed, most importantly in uncontrolled diabetes, but also in starvation and prolonged vomiting.

Complete explanation: Ketone bodies are produced in hepatic mitochondria from acetyl coenzyme A derived from fatty acids. β-hydroxybutyrate is quantitatively the main one in ketoacidosis, whereas the routine nitroprusside (Rothera) test detects acetoacetate and acetone only. They are normally used as fuel by muscle, heart and brain, and when production outstrips use they appear in blood (ketonaemia) and urine (ketonuria).

Causes of ketonuria:

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (insulin deficiency).
  • Starvation, prolonged fasting, very low carbohydrate diet.
  • Persistent vomiting (hyperemesis of pregnancy, pyloric stenosis) and severe diarrhoea.
  • Alcoholic ketoacidosis
    Febrile illness in children
    thyrotoxicosis.
  • Glycogen storage diseases, and treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
111:
Diabetic ketoacidosis develops when a profound deficiency of insulin, together with excess glucagon and other stress hormones, causes unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone production, together with severe hyperglycaemia and osmotic dehydration. It is mainly a complication of type 1 diabetes.

Complete explanation: The usual precipitant is omission of insulin, or infection, trauma or other stress. Epinephrine and other stress hormones antagonise residual insulin and stimulate glucagon secretion. The glucagon-to-insulin imbalance reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, so that plasma glucose rises to 250–600 mg/dL. Glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis, loss of water and electrolytes and dehydration.

Insulin deficiency also activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, which releases free fatty acids. In the liver these are converted to fatty acyl coenzyme A and oxidised to acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid. The rate of formation exceeds peripheral use, causing ketonaemia and ketonuria. When dehydration limits renal excretion of ketones, systemic metabolic acidosis results. Protein catabolism supplies ketogenic amino acids and aggravates the process.

Patients present with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath and Kussmaul respiration, and become drowsy and comatose if untreated. Ketoacidosis is less frequent in type 2 diabetes because the higher portal insulin level restrains hepatic fatty acid oxidation. Type 2 patients are more liable to a hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Treatment consists of insulin, fluid and electrolyte replacement and correction of the precipitating cause.
112:
Type 2 diabetes results from the combination of insulin resistance in peripheral tissues and a failure of the pancreatic β cells to compensate, producing relative insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility and obesity, especially visceral obesity, are the main determinants.

Complete explanation: There is no autoimmune basis.

Genetic factors. Concordance in monozygotic twins exceeds 90%, and first-degree relatives have a 5- to 10-fold increased risk. Genome-wide studies have identified more than 30 loci (such as TCF7L2) of modest effect, many involved in β-cell function, adipose tissue function and obesity.

Insulin resistance. Insulin resistance usually precedes hyperglycaemia. Its consequences are failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (high fasting glucose), reduced glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis in skeletal muscle after meals (high postprandial glucose), and uncontrolled lipolysis in adipose tissue (high free fatty acids). Defects include reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of the insulin receptor and IRS proteins and decreased GLUT-4 translocation.

Obesity contributes through several mechanisms: excess free fatty acids that generate toxic lipid intermediates (diacylglycerol, ceramides) and impair insulin signalling. Altered adipokines with lowered adiponectin
Chronic inflammation, in which fatty acids activate the inflammasome and release IL-1β and other cytokines. and hepatic steatosis (MASLD).

β-cell dysfunction. Initially the β cells hypersecrete and hyperinsulinaemia maintains euglycaemia. Eventually they fail, through lipotoxicity from excess fatty acids, glucotoxicity, a blunted incretin effect (reduced GIP and GLP-1 action), and islet amyloid deposition (found in over 90% of long-standing cases), together with genetic effects on insulin secretion.

Other risk factors are a sedentary lifestyle, sleep disorders and circadian disruption. The combination of obesity, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension is the metabolic syndrome.
113:
The macroscopic (macrovascular) complications of diabetes result from accelerated atherosclerosis of the aorta and large and medium-sized arteries, causing myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral vascular disease with gangrene. Hypoglycaemic coma is unconsciousness from a fall in blood glucose, usually due to excessive insulin or sulfonylurea dosage.

Complete explanation: Persistent hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance cause widespread endothelial dysfunction, which predisposes to atherosclerosis that is histologically identical to that in non-diabetics but occurs earlier and more severely. Hypertension and dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides and LDL, low HDL) potentiate it. Myocardial infarction is the most common cause of death in diabetes and is almost as common in diabetic women as in men. Cerebrovascular disease and renal artery atherosclerosis follow, and gangrene of the lower limbs is about 100 times more frequent than in the general population.

Gross renal changes include diffuse granular, contracted kidneys from arteriolosclerosis and nephrosclerosis, and pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis.

The microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) are due to diffuse basement-membrane thickening and increased capillary permeability.

Hypoglycaemic coma follows missed meals, exertion or inappropriate dosing. The patient is cold, pale and sweating with tachycardia and hunger, then confused and unconscious. It requires immediate oral or intravenous glucose, since prolonged hypoglycaemia causes permanent neuronal damage, especially of the cortex and hippocampus.
114:
Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the feature of hyperglycaemia caused by defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or most commonly both. By WHO and ADA criteria it is diagnosed by a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, a two-hour OGTT value or random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more with classic symptoms, or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more.

Complete explanation: The chronic hyperglycaemia causes secondary damage in the kidneys, eyes, nerves and blood vessels, and diabetes is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease, blindness and non-traumatic amputation. Diagnostic criteria (any one; all except a symptomatic random glucose must be confirmed on a separate day, and if two tests disagree the more abnormal result is accepted):

  1. Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).
  2. Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms.
  3. Two-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75 g OGTT.
  4. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.

Acute stresses such as infection, burns or trauma can cause transient hyperglycaemia, so persistence after recovery is required.
115:
These are the descriptive terms used for primary skin lesions. Macules and patches are flat lesions distinguished only by colour, the macule being less than 5 mm and the patch larger. Papules are solid elevations less than 5 mm. Vesicles and bullae are fluid-filled blisters, smaller and larger than 5 mm respectively. A pustule is a pus-filled elevation, and a wheal is a transient, oedematous, pale-pink raised plaque.

Complete explanation: Dermatopathology begins with a precise clinical vocabulary, because the distribution and character of a lesion often point to the diagnosis before any tissue is examined.

A plaque is the larger counterpart of the papule: an elevated, flat-topped lesion greater than 5 mm in diameter, usually produced by confluent papules. The size limit of 5 mm is the conventional dividing line between each small and large pair.
116:
The skin consists of the epidermis, the dermis and the subcutis, with appendages such as hair follicles and sweat and sebaceous glands. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium of basal, spinous, granular and cornified layers. Parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, hypergranulosis is thickening of the granular layer, acanthosis is thickening of the epidermis from hyperplasia of the spinous layer, and spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis.

Complete explanation

Structure of the skin. The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium whose principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves upward from the basal layer. The deepest layer, the stratum basale, is a single row of cuboidal cells attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes. it contains the proliferating stem cells. Above it lies the stratum spinosum, whose cells are joined by desmosomes, giving the spiny appearance on fixation.

Next is the stratum granulosum, with coarse basophilic keratohyalin granules that contribute to the cornified envelope. The outermost layer, the stratum corneum, consists of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames that form the barrier. on the palms and soles a clear stratum lucidum may be identified. Interspersed among the keratinocytes are melanocytes in the basal layer, which transfer melanin to neighbouring keratinocytes and protect the nuclei from ultraviolet radiation, Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting dendritic cells in the spinous layer, and Merkel cells, which are touch-related neuroendocrine cells.

The epidermis is separated from the dermis by the basement membrane zone, which anchors it and whose components (hemidesmosomal proteins, laminin, type VII collagen) are targeted in several blistering diseases. The dermis has a superficial papillary layer of loose connective tissue containing capillary loops, and a deeper, denser reticular layer of thick collagen bundles and elastic fibres, with blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves and sensory receptors.

The subcutis is composed of lobules of fat separated by fibrous septa. The appendages (pilosebaceous units, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands, and nails) arise from the epidermis and extend into the dermis.

Descriptive terms

  • Parakeratosis is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. It indicates rapid epidermal turnover with incomplete maturation of keratinocytes, and it is accompanied by a thin or absent granular layer, as in psoriasis.
  • Hypergranulosis is an increase in the thickness of the stratum granulosum, usually a response to chronic rubbing or scratching, and a prominent feature of lichen planus.
  • Acanthosis is diffuse epithelial hyperplasia, with thickening of the stratum spinosum, and is a common response to chronic irritation or growth factors.
  • Spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis. The oedema stretches the intercellular bridges so that the keratinocytes are pulled apart. it is the hallmark of eczematous dermatitis, and when severe it forms intraepidermal vesicles.

Related terms that complete the group are hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum), acantholysis (loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes, as in pemphigus), and dyskeratosis (premature, abnormal keratinisation of individual cells).
117:
The blistering diseases of the skin are classified by the level at which the blister forms. Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus form intraepidermal blisters through acantholysis. Bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa and porphyria cutanea tarda form subepidermal blisters. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and impetigo produce subcorneal blisters.

Complete explanation: In vesiculobullous disease, a blister arises either within the epidermis, from damage to desmosomes and keratinocyte cohesion, or beneath it, from damage to the basement membrane zone. The distinction is clinically important because intraepidermal blisters have a thin roof and rupture easily, producing erosions, whereas subepidermal blisters have a full-thickness roof and remain tense and intact.

118:
The important premalignant conditions of the skin are actinic (solar) keratosis, Bowen disease, arsenical and radiation keratoses, xeroderma pigmentosum, leukoplakia of mucosal surfaces, long-standing scars and chronic ulcers, and the dysplastic naevus.

Complete explanation: Many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, and a proportion of melanomas, arise from recognisable precursor lesions in which cumulative DNA damage has already produced cytological atypia.

  • Actinic keratosis is the commonest premalignant lesion. It appears on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned older people as a small, rough, scaly erythematous or brown patch. Microscopically there is atypia of the basal keratinocytes with parakeratosis and solar elastosis in the dermis. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is uncommon for any single lesion but cumulatively significant.
  • Bowen disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ, with full-thickness epidermal atypia but an intact basement membrane.
  • Arsenical keratosis and radiation dermatitis result from chemical or ionising carcinogen exposure and are followed by squamous carcinoma after a long latent interval.
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive defect of nucleotide excision repair, producing multiple cancers at a young age on exposure to sunlight.
  • Leukoplakia and lichen sclerosus of the oral or genital mucosa carry a risk of squamous carcinoma.
  • Chronic scars, burn scars, sinus tracts and non-healing ulcers may give rise to squamous carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).
  • Dysplastic naevus, particularly in the familial dysplastic naevus syndrome, is both a marker of increased risk and a precursor of melanoma.
119:
The important tumours of the skin include benign tumours such as seborrhoeic keratosis, naevi, adnexal tumours and dermatofibroma, and malignant tumours such as squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and malignant melanoma, together with Kaposi sarcoma and cutaneous lymphoma. The locally malignant tumour of the skin is basal cell carcinoma.

Complete explanation: Skin tumours may be grouped according to the cell of origin.

Basal cell carcinoma is the locally malignant tumour of the skin. It invades and destroys adjacent tissue (rodent ulcer) and recurs after inadequate excision, but it very rarely metastasises.
120:
Basal cell carcinoma is a distinctive, locally aggressive cutaneous tumour associated with mutations that activate the Hedgehog signalling pathway. It is the commonest cancer in humans and is locally invasive but rarely metastasises. It occurs mainly on sun-exposed skin of the face, especially the nose, cheeks, forehead and inner canthus. Grossly it is a pearly papule with telangiectasia that may ulcerate, and microscopically it shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading.

Complete explanation: Basal cell carcinoma arises from the basal cells of the epidermis and follicular epithelium, and in the great majority of cases it is associated with cumulative exposure to ultraviolet light. It is more frequent in fair-skinned people, in those with xeroderma pigmentosum, in chronic arsenic exposure and in immunosuppression. Most cases carry mutations in the Hedgehog signalling pathway, usually inactivating PTCH1
Germline PTCH1 mutations underlie the basal cell naevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), characterised by multiple basal cell carcinomas appearing early, jaw keratocysts and skeletal abnormalities. TP53 mutations arising from UV damage are also frequent.

Sites. Tumours occur on hair-bearing, sun-exposed skin, particularly the face (nose, inner canthus, cheeks, forehead and upper lip), the ears and the scalp. The palms, soles and mucosal surfaces are only rarely involved.

Morphology. Grossly, the lesion begins as a small, pearly, dome-shaped papule with prominent overlying telangiectatic vessels. It enlarges slowly and may ulcerate centrally, leaving a crusted ulcer with a raised, rolled, pearly edge (rodent ulcer). Some tumours contain melanin and appear brown or black, and a sclerosing form resembles a scar.

Microscopically, the tumour consists of nests, cords and islands of basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm, resembling the cells of the normal basal layer, within a stroma. The cells at the periphery of each nest are arranged in a regular, palisading fashion, while those in the centre are haphazardly arranged. A characteristic retraction space (cleft) separates the tumour nests from the surrounding mucinous stroma.

Mitoses and apoptotic cells are usually numerous. The tumour often grows in the superficial, nodular, infiltrative or sclerosing (morpheaform) patterns, the last two being more aggressive and more likely to recur.

Behaviour. The tumour grows slowly, destroying the skin, cartilage and even bone, notably around the eye and nose, but metastasis is extremely rare. Complete excision, Mohs surgery or radiotherapy is curative in most cases.
121:
Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the skin, and squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common. Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant tumour of keratinocytes. Grossly it is a crusted, scaly, ulcerated nodule on sun-exposed skin, and microscopically it shows invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls.

Complete explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest skin malignancy overall. Squamous cell carcinoma is the second commonest, although in people with darker skin pigmentation it is often the more frequent skin cancer.

Squamous cell carcinoma occurs mainly in older people on sun-exposed skin: the face, ears, scalp, lower lip, dorsum of the hands and forearms. Other causes are chronic arsenic ingestion, ionising radiation, tar and oil exposure, chronic ulcers, burn scars and draining sinus tracts, immunosuppression (especially after organ transplantation) and human papillomavirus infection in the anogenital region. UV light is the principal factor, producing characteristic mutations in TP53 and others.

Morphology. The earliest lesion is the in situ carcinoma (Bowen disease or its precursor actinic keratosis), presenting grossly as a sharply defined, red, scaly plaque, and microscopically as full-thickness atypia of the epidermal cells with an intact basement membrane. When the tumour becomes invasive, the gross appearance is of a firm, keratotic, crusted, nodular lesion which tends to ulcerate, forming an ulcer with an indurated, raised, everted edge.

Microscopically, the invasive tumour consists of irregular nests, cords and sheets of atypical squamous epithelial cells, which infiltrate the dermis and sometimes deeper tissues. Well-differentiated tumours form keratin pearls and show prominent intercellular bridges, with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Poorly differentiated tumours show greater nuclear pleomorphism, numerous mitoses including atypical forms, little keratinisation, and sometimes a spindled pattern.

Behaviour. Metastasis, chiefly to regional lymph nodes, is much more likely than for basal cell carcinoma, but still uncommon for tumours arising in sun-damaged skin. The risk is greater for tumours that arise on the lip, ear, or in scars, burns, irradiated skin or the immunosuppressed, and for large, deep and poorly differentiated tumours or those with perineural invasion.
122:
The most probable diagnosis is a squamous cell carcinoma of the great toe with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes. The main alternative is a malignant melanoma, particularly the acral or subungual type, and a chronic ulcer with reactive lymphadenitis must be excluded. I would confirm the diagnosis by biopsy of the ulcer edge and FNAC or biopsy of the inguinal node, followed by staging investigations.

Complete explanation: An elderly man with a six-month non-healing ulcer on the toe that has recently begun to spread, together with an enlarging swelling in the ipsilateral groin, which is the first-station nodal group for the lower limb, has a cutaneous malignancy with nodal metastasis until proven otherwise.

Probable diagnoses

  1. Squamous cell carcinoma of the toe, possibly arising in a chronic ulcer, a scar or a site of trauma (Marjolin ulcer), with inguinal nodal metastasis.
  2. Malignant melanoma (acral lentiginous or ulcerated nodular type), which can also be ulcerated and spreads to inguinal nodes.
  3. Less likely: Kaposi sarcoma, a chronic diabetic, venous, arterial or trophic ulcer with reactive lymphadenitis, a tuberculous or fungal ulcer, and a pigmented or ulcerated basal cell carcinoma, which is unusual at this site.

Investigations

  • Biopsy of the edge of the ulcer, including adjacent normal skin, for histology. Immunohistochemistry (cytokeratin, p63 or p40 for squamous carcinoma; S100, HMB-45, Melan-A or SOX10 for melanoma) to settle the diagnosis.
  • FNAC or excision biopsy of the inguinal lymph node to confirm metastasis.
  • Imaging: X-ray of the foot to detect bone invasion
    Ultrasonography, CT or MRI of the groin and pelvis for deep (iliac) nodes. Chest X-ray or CT, and abdominal imaging or PET-CT, for distant metastases.
  • Laboratory tests: complete blood count, ESR, blood glucose (to exclude diabetes), liver and renal function tests, and serum LDH if melanoma is confirmed.
  • Bacteriological culture of the ulcer if infection is suspected.
123:
A naevus is a benign, localised proliferation of melanocytes, commonly called a mole. The principal types are the acquired melanocytic naevi (junctional, compound and intradermal), congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus and the dysplastic naevus.

Complete explanation: The term naevus denotes any congenital or acquired benign localised proliferation of melanocytes (naevus cells) in the skin. Acquired melanocytic naevi are extremely common, appearing in childhood and early adulthood. Most carry the activating BRAF V600E mutation. Proliferation is limited by oncogene-induced senescence, and so most naevi remain small and stable and later involute.

Types

  1. Common acquired naevus. This is a small (usually less than 6 mm), symmetric, uniformly tan to dark-brown, sharply circumscribed macule or papule. It evolves through three histological stages.
    • Junctional naevus: nests of naevus cells at the dermoepidermal junction. a flat, brown macule.
    • Compound naevus: nests at the junction and in the dermis
      a raised papule.
    • Intradermal naevus: nests and cords only in the dermis
      a dome-shaped, often skin-coloured papule. The cells become smaller with increasing depth ("maturation").
  2. Congenital naevus: present at birth, often larger, with naevus cells extending deep around adnexa. Giant forms carry a small risk of melanoma.
  3. Blue naevus: a dark blue papule of heavily pigmented dermal spindle melanocytes.
  4. Spitz naevus: a pink, dome-shaped nodule in children, with large epithelioid and spindle cells. it can be mistaken for melanoma.
  5. Dysplastic naevus: larger than common naevi (generally more than 5 mm), with irregular borders and variegated colour
    it shows architectural disorder, cytological atypia and lamellar fibroplasia. It is a marker of, and a precursor to, melanoma, especially in the familial dysplastic naevus syndrome (CDKN2A mutations).
124:
Malignant melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes. Grossly it is an asymmetrical pigmented lesion with irregular borders, variegated colour and a diameter often greater than 6 mm. Microscopically it consists of large atypical melanocytes with prominent nucleoli, growing as nests and single cells at all levels of the epidermis and invading the dermis. It passes from a radial to a vertical growth phase, and the depth of invasion determines prognosis.

Complete explanation: Melanoma arises from epidermal melanocytes, chiefly in the skin, and is related to intense intermittent sun exposure, fair skin, numerous naevi, a family history, and inherited mutations in CDKN2A. Acquired mutations of BRAF, NRAS and KIT drive many tumours, and acral and mucosal melanomas are more often KIT-mutant.

Gross morphology. Melanomas are recognised by the "ABCDE" features: Asymmetry, Border irregularity (notched and scalloped), Colour variegation (shades of brown, black, red, blue and white where there is regression), Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolution or enlargement. The surface may be elevated, and ulceration occurs in advanced lesions.

Microscopic morphology. There are two phases of growth. In the radial growth phase, malignant cells spread horizontally within the epidermis and superficial papillary dermis. The cells are usually large, with abundant cytoplasm containing fine melanin dust, large, pleomorphic, irregular nuclei, and prominent, eosinophilic ("cherry-red") nucleoli. They form nests of varying size and spread as single cells upward through all epidermal levels (pagetoid spread).

Cells in this phase generally do not have metastatic potential. In the vertical growth phase, the tumour cells invade the deeper dermis as an expansile nodule or as sheets, with mitotic figures, and acquire the capacity to metastasise.

Clinical subtypes. Superficial spreading melanoma is the commonest. Lentigo maligna melanoma occurs on the sun-damaged face of the elderly. Nodular melanoma has a vertical growth phase from the start and is aggressive. Acral lentiginous melanoma occurs on the palms, soles and under the nails, and is the commonest type in dark-skinned populations.

Prognosis. The single most important prognostic factor is the Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in millimetres), followed by ulceration, mitotic rate and regional lymph node status. Melanoma metastasises to regional lymph nodes and then to the lungs, liver, brain and bone. Tumour cells are positive for S100, HMB-45, Melan-A and SOX10.
125:
The probable diagnosis is malignant melanoma of the acral lentiginous type, arising on the sole of the foot, with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes.

Complete explanation: An elderly man with a rapidly changing, blackish pigmented and ulcerated lesion on the sole, which is a classical site of acral lentiginous melanoma, and a new swelling in the ipsilateral groin, the first-order nodal station for the foot, most probably has a malignant melanoma with regional lymph node metastasis. Pigmentation (the black colour from melanin), rapid growth and ulceration, which means vertical growth phase and a thick tumour, all support this diagnosis.

Acral melanoma is not related to sun exposure and is the commonest type in dark-skinned populations
The delay in diagnosis, because the lesion is hidden on the sole, explains why such cases usually present late with nodal spread.

Differential diagnoses include squamous cell carcinoma of the sole, Kaposi sarcoma, pigmented basal cell carcinoma (very rare at this site), a plantar wart or pyogenic granuloma with haemorrhage, a subcutaneous haematoma, and a chronic trophic ulcer with a pigmented margin. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy with immunohistochemistry (S100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10), and the inguinal swelling by FNAC or biopsy
Breslow thickness and the nodal status stage the disease.
126:

A malignant melanoma is larger and asymmetrical, with an irregular border and variegated colour, and microscopically shows atypical melanocytes with prominent nucleoli, mitoses and invasion, without maturation.

127:
Osteomyelitis is inflammation of the bone and marrow, almost always due to infection. The commonest cause is Staphylococcus aureus, and bacteria reach bone by haematogenous spread, by extension from a contiguous focus, or by direct implantation after trauma or surgery. It is classified as acute or chronic, and by aetiology as pyogenic or tuberculous. In chronic osteomyelitis, a sequestrum is a fragment of dead bone, an involucrum is the new bone formed around it, and Brodie abscess is a small walled-off intraosseous abscess.

Complete explanation

Definition. Osteomyelitis is an inflammatory process of bone and bone marrow caused by infection. It is a clinical and pathological term for infection, usually bacterial, that may be acute or chronic.

Causes. The causative organism is usually a pyogenic bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus accounts for most cases, and is the commonest agent at all ages. Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella are associated with genitourinary tract infection and intravenous drug use. Haemophilus influenzae and group B streptococci cause neonatal infection, and Salmonella is a classic cause in patients with sickle cell disease. Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculous osteomyelitis, and fungi and other organisms may be responsible in the immunocompromised.

Routes of entry. (1) Haematogenous spread from a distant focus (the most common route, especially in children), (2) direct extension from an adjacent focus of infection, such as a diabetic foot ulcer, a sinus or an infected joint, and (3) direct implantation through compound fractures or surgery.

Classification. By duration, it is acute or chronic. By cause, it is pyogenic (bacterial), tuberculous, or due to other organisms such as fungi and syphilis. By route, it is haematogenous, contiguous or post-traumatic.

Morphology of chronic osteomyelitis. Chronic osteomyelitis follows incompletely treated acute infection, or arises as a primary chronic infection. The central feature is necrotic bone, which is the persistent focus of infection because it cannot be penetrated by inflammatory cells and antibiotics. Around the dead bone is chronic inflammatory tissue (lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages) with fibrosis and granulation tissue, and new reactive bone is laid down by the periosteum.

A sinus tract (cloaca) may discharge pus through the involucrum and the skin. Radiologically, the sequestrum appears as a dense fragment surrounded by a radiolucent zone with thickened sclerotic bone.

Sequestrum, involucrum and Brodie abscess. The sequestrum is a segment of necrotic bone, separated from the living bone by granulation tissue and suppuration. The involucrum is a sleeve of new bone formed by the periosteum around the infected, necrotic bone. it may have openings (cloacae) through which pus drains. Brodie abscess is a small (usually 1–4 cm) intraosseous abscess walled off by reactive sclerotic bone, usually in the metaphysis of the tibia, representing a subacute or chronic infection with a low-virulence organism.
128:
Bone tumours are classified according to the tissue they produce into bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic and tumours of unknown origin, each with benign and malignant examples. Pott disease is tuberculosis of the spine, with vertebral destruction, kyphosis and a cold abscess.

Complete explanation

Metastases are the commonest malignant tumours of bone overall. Among primary bone tumours, myeloma is the commonest, followed by osteosarcoma.

Pott disease is tuberculous osteomyelitis of the vertebral column. Haematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae causes caseating granulomatous destruction of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs. Vertebral collapse causes kyphosis (gibbus), a cold abscess may track along the psoas sheath to the groin, and cord compression may cause paraplegia.
129:
The bone-forming tumours are osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour apart from myeloma. It most often arises in the metaphysis of long bones around the knee, particularly the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia. It is a bulky gritty tumour that microscopically produces neoplastic osteoid and bone, and radiologically shows Codman triangle and a sunburst pattern.

Complete explanation

Bone-forming tumours. These are osteoma, osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma, which are benign, and osteosarcoma, which is malignant.

Osteosarcoma. It is a malignant mesenchymal tumour in which the neoplastic cells produce osteoid and bone. It has a peak incidence in adolescents and young adults between 10 and 20 years, and a second smaller peak in the elderly, in whom it is associated with Paget disease of bone, bone infarcts and prior irradiation. It is more frequent in males. Predisposing genetic factors are inactivating mutations of RB1 (hereditary retinoblastoma) and TP53 (Li–Fraumeni syndrome)
CDK4 and MDM2 amplification also occurs.

Site. The tumour typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, with about 60% of tumours around the knee, in the distal femur and proximal tibia. The proximal humerus is the next commonest site.

Gross morphology. A large, gritty, grey-white, often haemorrhagic and necrotic tumour that arises in the metaphysis and frequently destroys the cortex, lifts the periosteum and forms a soft tissue mass. It extends through the marrow cavity but usually spares the epiphyseal cartilage, although it may extend into the epiphysis and sometimes the joint.

Microscopic morphology. The tumour is composed of pleomorphic, malignant cells, often with hyperchromatic, bizarre nuclei, atypical mitoses and giant cells. The essential diagnostic feature is the formation of neoplastic osteoid (and bone) directly by the tumour cells, which appears as lace-like, eosinophilic matrix. Matrix may be mineralised and appear as a fine, lace-like deposit around tumour cells. Variants include osteoblastic, chondroblastic, fibroblastic, telangiectatic and small cell patterns.

Radiology. The radiograph shows a destructive, mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion in the metaphysis, with an ill-defined margin, soft tissue extension, elevation of the periosteum that appears as Codman triangle, and radiating bone spicules, giving a "sunburst" appearance.

Clinical features. Painful progressive swelling, and sometimes a pathological fracture, with raised serum alkaline phosphatase. It metastasises early by the blood stream, mainly to the lungs. Treatment is neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-sparing surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The 5-year survival is about 60–70% in the absence of metastasis at presentation.
130:
Bone tumours are classified as bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic, and those of unknown origin, such as giant cell tumour and Ewing sarcoma. Giant cell tumour of bone typically occurs in the epiphysis of long bones in adults aged 20 to 40. Microscopically it consists of mononuclear stromal cells with scattered multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, and it is locally aggressive.

Complete explanation

Classification. Bone tumours are grouped by the type of tissue they differentiate towards. Bone-forming tumours include osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma and osteosarcoma. Cartilage-forming tumours include osteochondroma, enchondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma and chondrosarcoma. Fibrous and fibro-osseous lesions include fibrous cortical defect, non-ossifying fibroma and fibrous dysplasia. The tumours of uncertain origin are giant cell tumour and Ewing sarcoma. Others include chordoma, vascular tumours, myeloma and lymphoma, and metastatic tumours.

Giant cell tumour of bone. It is a locally aggressive tumour that occurs in young adults between 20 and 40 years of age, slightly more often in women. The tumour arises in the epiphysis (extending into the metaphysis) of long bones, most commonly at the lower end of the femur, upper end of the tibia and lower end of the radius.

Gross. The tumour is large, soft, red-brown and haemorrhagic, often with cystic degeneration and areas of necrosis. It expands the end of the bone, thins and erodes the cortex, and may extend into the soft tissue and, rarely, into the joint.

Microscopic. The tumour consists of sheets of uniform, round to oval mononuclear stromal cells, which are the neoplastic element, among which are numerous evenly distributed multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells with many nuclei that resemble the nuclei of the stromal cells. The mononuclear cells show little pleomorphism and moderate mitotic activity. The giant cells are recruited by RANKL expressed by the stromal cells. Haemorrhage, haemosiderin deposition, foamy macrophages and reactive woven bone are frequent. The tumour cells carry mutations of H3F3A (G34W).

Radiology and behaviour. A purely lytic, eccentric, expansile "soap-bubble" lesion extending to the subchondral bone. Recurrence after curettage occurs in 40–60%, and a few tumours metastasise to the lungs. Treatment is curettage or excision, and denosumab, an antibody to RANKL, is used for unresectable tumours.
131:
Bone tumours are classified into bone-forming, cartilage-forming, fibrous, vascular, haematopoietic and tumours of uncertain origin, and each includes benign and malignant tumours. Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumour of bone, occurring in children and adolescents, characterised by the t(11;22) translocation producing the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene.

Complete explanation

Classification. Bone tumours are classified as bone-forming (osteoma, osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, osteosarcoma), cartilage-forming (osteochondroma, enchondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, chondrosarcoma), fibrous (fibrous cortical defect, non-ossifying fibroma, fibrosarcoma), tumours of uncertain origin (giant cell tumour, Ewing sarcoma), vascular (haemangioma, angiosarcoma), haematopoietic (myeloma, lymphoma), notochordal (chordoma) and metastatic tumours.

Ewing sarcoma. This is a primitive malignant tumour of small round cells showing neuroectodermal differentiation, and it is the second most common bone sarcoma of childhood. It occurs mainly in the first two decades (peak around 10–15 years) and more often in boys. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones such as the femur, tibia and humerus, and also in the pelvis and ribs. More than 90% carry the translocation t(11;22)(q24;q12), creating the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene, which acts as an aberrant transcription factor.

Gross. A soft, tan-white tumour arising in the medullary cavity, with haemorrhage and necrosis, which invades the cortex and extends into the soft tissue.

Microscopic. Sheets of uniform small round cells, slightly larger than lymphocytes, with scanty, clear to pale cytoplasm that is rich in glycogen (PAS-positive) and round nuclei with fine chromatin, with few mitoses. Homer Wright rosettes are found in some cases. The tumour cells express CD99 (MIC2) strongly.

Clinical. Local pain and swelling, which may be accompanied by fever, leucocytosis and raised ESR, mimicking osteomyelitis. Radiography shows a destructive, permeative lytic lesion with lamellated "onion-skin" periosteal reaction. The tumour is chemosensitive, and treatment with chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy gives 5-year survival of about 70–75% for localised disease.
132:
Soft tissue refers to all non-epithelial extraskeletal tissues of the body, excluding the viscera, the coverings of the brain, and the haematopoietic and lymphoid tissues. Examples of soft tissue tumours are lipoma and liposarcoma, fibroma and fibrosarcoma, leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, haemangioma, neurofibroma and synovial sarcoma.

Complete explanation: Soft tissue comprises fat, fibrous tissue, skeletal and smooth muscle, blood vessels, peripheral nerve sheaths and synovium, which are mesenchymal in origin, and it excludes the viscera, the meninges, the haematopoietic and lymphoid tissues, and the skeleton. Tumours are named after the tissue to which they show differentiation, and are divided into benign tumours, whose suffix is "-oma", and malignant tumours, called sarcomas.

They tend to grow as expansile masses with a pseudocapsule, and they spread mainly by the blood stream, to the lungs, rather than through lymphatics. Their grade, depth, size and resectability determine prognosis.
136:
Meningitis is inflammation of the leptomeninges, the pia and arachnoid, with an inflammatory exudate in the cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space. It may be acute pyogenic (bacterial), aseptic (usually viral) or chronic (tuberculous or fungal). The causative organisms depend on the age of the patient: Escherichia coli and group B streptococci in neonates, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae in infants and children, and N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae in adolescents, adults and the elderly.

Complete explanation: Meningitis is defined as inflammation of the leptomeninges and of the subarachnoid CSF. Microorganisms reach the meninges mostly by the haematogenous route, from an infected focus such as the nasopharynx or lung, and less often by direct spread from otitis media, mastoiditis or sinusitis, by direct implantation through a skull fracture or neurosurgery, or by a congenital neural tube defect. Because the CSF has little immune defence, bacteria that enter it multiply freely, and the inflammatory response, rather than the organism alone, produces much of the damage.

Microscopically there are neutrophils in the subarachnoid space, and in severe cases the exudate extends along the perivascular spaces and causes ventriculitis, vasculitis, thrombophlebitis and cerebral oedema. Complications include hydrocephalus, cerebral infarction, and cranial nerve palsies. Clinically there is fever, headache, photophobia, irritability, neck stiffness and altered consciousness.
133:
Tumours of the central nervous system are classified by their cell of origin into gliomas (astrocytic, oligodendroglial and ependymal), neuronal and glioneuronal tumours, choroid plexus tumours, embryonal tumours such as medulloblastoma, tumours of the meninges, nerve sheath tumours, germ cell tumours, primary CNS lymphoma, sellar tumours, and metastases. Their peculiarities are that the site matters more than the histological grade, that benign tumours can be lethal because of the closed cranium, that infiltrating gliomas cannot be cured by excision, and that they rarely metastasise outside the CNS but may spread through the CSF.

Complete explanation
